Large language models have evolved from single-turn chatbots into interactive agents capable of long-horizon reasoning. In real deployments, MCP tool services can return noisy feedback and users may intervene to correct the agent, but existing methods provide limited supervision for reflection learning and failure recovery. To bridge this gap, we propose Agent-Reflex, a general training framework for incentivizing proactive reflection in agents. Specifically, Agent-Reflex comprises three stages. First, Environment Reflection Skill Discovery (RSD) injects grounded tool-feedback perturbations into environment scaling, samples a capability-diverse LLM pool, mines matched success-failure pairs, and summarizes reusable reflection meta-skills. Building on this skill library, we then apply Reflective Supervised Fine-Tuning (ReSFT) that converts each skill into supervision for self-reflection, skill recovery, and user-centric correction, strengthening complementary reflective behaviors. Finally, we propose On-Policy Reflective Policy Optimization (ORPO) to combine agentic reinforcement learning under noisy interactions with reflection-guided on-policy distillation to further elicit proactive reflection. Built on Qwen3-8B, Agent-Reflex reaches 58.6 overall on five long-horizon tool-use benchmarks and 29.1 on AgentNoiseBench, surpassing strong environment-scaling and reflection baselines. Experiments on six challenging agent benchmark suites demonstrate the effectiveness of Agent-Reflex. Further analyses show that Agent-Reflex improves agents' robustness to noise while maintaining stable training dynamics, supporting scalable agent training. Our code is available at https://github.com/RUC-NLPIR/Agent-Reflex.

Human-robot collaboration has relied on task models that are specified in advance for each product. Embodied foundation models and agentic artificial intelligence change this premise, because a robot can now interpret an open goal, plan, act, monitor the outcome and recover from failure. This review examines what that change means for collaboration. A critical narrative review was conducted over 231 sources. Embodied intelligence, agentic intelligence, autonomy and collaboration are distinguished, and four collaboration modes are defined by the roles of the human and the robot. Four system architectures are compared: modular agentic, end-to-end embodied, hierarchical agentic embodied, and human-centred shared autonomy. Six groups of enabling technologies and five collaboration mechanisms, from autonomy allocation to failure recovery, are analysed. Applications in six domains, from manufacturing to domestic service, are assessed by the maturity of their evidence. Reported systems are validated mainly on single cells and short tasks, human factors are measured in few studies, and verified safety layers remain separate from learned reasoning. An evaluation framework and research directions for seven open challenges are proposed. The review gives researchers and system builders a basis for bringing embodied and agentic AI into human-robot collaboration and for evaluating the systems that result.

Can an AI agent turn high-level user intent into a functioning robot and teach it how to behave? We study this question from two complementary aspects: embodiment and behavior creation. For embodiment creation, we investigate how well current multimodal models capture mechanical requirements, and introduce computational metrics for evaluating generated designs before fabrication. For behavior creation, we present Roboforge, an agentic framework that turns task specifications into executable policies through motion generation, policy learning, and execution-grounded revision. Given a robot embodiment and task, the agent generates a reference motion, configures the learning objective, and trains a policy. Crucially, motion remains in the loop: rollout feedback can revise the reference motion, reward, or both. We evaluate a generated embodiment across multiple MLLMs and behavior creation across four diverse robots against reward-refinement and one-shot motion baselines. Our computational metrics expose recurring mechanical failures in generated designs, while behavior experiments show that execution-grounded refinement improves task-level behavior and execution quality. Finally, we fabricate an agent-generated Gorilla and directly deploy learned behaviors on the physical robot.

Benchmarks report what an Artificial Intelligence (AI) agent can do on a task suite, but not whether one released version has been engineered with the controls that make it reliable, safe and observable, or how strongly that is shown. This paper proposes AgentStripes, an evidence-graded maturity model for AI agents. It defines levels (0 to 7 stripes), process areas (12 areas holding 40 capabilities), three gates (basic, safety, proof) that hold an agent at a level however high its score, and evidence grades E0 to E5. Each applicable capability receives a rating from 0 to 3 and a separate evidence level; these are combined into a credit, aggregated into a severity-weighted score and converted into stripes that the gates limit. Instruments gather evidence, language-model judges interpret it under explicit criteria, and the arithmetic is deterministic. The model is compared with standards at topic level without a claim of conformance, and an unexecuted validation protocol is specified. An empirical evaluation (exploratory, non-confirmatory) of 30 public Python agent repositories, with static evidence only, is a demonstration and not a validation: static evidence caps every final stripe at 2, 26 repositories end at one stripe and 4 at two, and this distinction is unreliable, since re-judging changed the final stripe of 4 of 22 repositories (engine, dossier and panel changed), whereas none of 8 panel-only repeats, all at stripe 1, changed. The parameters are expert conventions without outcome based calibration, and the stripes have not been shown to predict reliability or safety.

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being applied across neuro-oncology domains to analyze complex, high-dimensional, multimodal data. Despite major advances in the biological understanding and classification of CNS tumors, clinical outcomes for many of them remain poor, reflecting intra- and inter-tumor heterogeneity and limitations of conventional reductionist approaches. AI offers a paradigm shift to capture this heterogeneity and provide quantitative, reproducible diagnostic, predictive, and prognostic insights. This article describes a joint effort across the Response Assessment in Neuro-Oncology (RANO) working groups to provide an overarching review of the AI use across six key domains of neuro-oncology: neuroimaging, neuropathology, laboratory medicine, neurosurgery, drug discovery, and clinical trials. Applications closest to clinical use include imaging segmentation and quantification, AI-assisted image reconstruction, DNA methylation-based classification, and workflow optimization. Radiogenomics, WSI-based molecular prediction, AI-guided surgical targeting, liquid biopsy interpretation, AI-guided drug discovery, digital twins, and in silico trials remain promising but require stronger prospective validation. Key challenges include limited availability of large diverse datasets, variability in data acquisition and reference standards, and limited external validation. This review provides a unifying framework for understanding the role of AI across neuro-oncology and highlights key considerations for its responsible implementation, emphasizing standardization, reproducibility, multi-institutional validation, and human oversight.

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming increasingly mainstream in children's homes and everyday lives. Using neo-ecological theory as a conceptual framework and Yang et al.'s (2026) five-component AI literacy progression model as an analytical lens, this document analysis examined core ECEC curricula and related guiding documents currently in use in Australia, China, Japan, and South Korea to determine whether early childhood education and care (ECEC) guiding documents are keeping pace with the rapid development. The analysis reveals that the curricula of Japan and South Korea contain no explicit reference to AI literacy, prioritising human-to-human relationships and offline safety. China's national ECEC guidelines similarly contain no AI references. However, Shanghai's strategic action plan explicitly positions kindergartens within broader AI education initiatives, though without specifying pedagogical progressions for young learners. Australia demonstrates limited and uneven alignment across AI literacy components, with the strongest alignment in “Interacting with AI Agents” and no alignment in “Understanding Human-AI Relationships”. Young children’s development of AI literacy is thus likely to remain contingent on the home environment, where they may be interacting with AI agents and creating artefacts more than developing awareness of ethical considerations and risks. Wide differences in children's foundational AI literacy capabilities may entrench educational disadvantage along the lines of AI literacy as it becomes increasingly mainstream in society. We argue that curriculum-guiding documents should be strengthened by articulating explicit AI literacy learning priorities and developmental expectations for young children, accompanied by culturally responsive resources to equip educators to facilitate equitable learning.

documents.abstract: Extension lacks literature comparing standalone generative artificial intelligence (AI) with structured professional development for capacity building. Guided by Social Cognitive Theory and Cognitive Load Theory, this study evaluated the effects of an asynchronous online course and a custom AI tutor on evaluation knowledge and self-efficacy among Cooperative Extension professionals. We conducted a randomized 2 × 2 factorial pilot study crossing access to an evaluation certificate course with access to a custom Generative Pre-trained Transformer (GPT). Of 144 registrants, 78 provided matched pre- and post-test data, with attrition differing across conditions. Data were analyzed using a three-way mixed factorial ANOVA. Course access and GPT access each increased objective knowledge, with post-test means around 91% across treatment groups. No statistically significant additive effect was detected for knowledge gain. However, given a possible ceiling effect and limited statistical power, this result is inconclusive. Course access and GPT access each increased self-efficacy, but the combined condition produced the smallest self-efficacy gain among treatment groups. Because these estimates are based on participants who completed the study, findings are preliminary. If replicated, results suggest that Extension should combine AI tutors and coursework only when each modality provides known complementary value.

documents.abstract: Learning Management Systems (LMSs) are widely used to organize learning materials, communication, assessment, and progress tracking. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) creates opportunities to make these systems more responsive to learners’ needs. This thesis examines two related applications: personalized learning support and automated assessment. It outlines how AI can use learning activity data to recommend suitable resources, identify topics that may require additional practice, and provide timely feedback. The paper also discusses limitations associated with data privacy, algorithmic bias, transparency, and the need for teacher oversight. The study is conceptual and based on a review of relevant literature; it does not report original experimental measurements. It concludes that AI can support teaching and learning when it is implemented as an assistive tool within a transparent, privacy-aware, and educator-supervised LMS.

documents.abstract: The development and use of artificial intelligence (AI) tools such as ChatGPT have raised concerns about assessment practice in higher education (HE). Prior studies have discussed the need to re-imagine and re-design assessment instruments; however, there is limited empirical evidence on how to effectively deploy this in practice. This paper proposes the TSD (task, scaffolding support and deliverable) framework to guide academics and education providers on how to effectively integrate AI and reflective practice into assessment design. By doing so, we adopt a mixed-method approach to investigate educational outcomes, tutors’ and students’ perspectives on the reflective AI-enabled assessment. This study collected data from UK University students (22 respondents) and tutors (24 participants) using a survey questionnaire and semi-structured interview questions, respectively. This study provides empirical support for positioning reflective practice as evidence of learning rather than being treated as a mere assessment activity. The findings show that AI output verification specific tasks need to be incorporated into AI-enabled assessment design. The results suggest that students perceived that our assessment strategy encouraged deeper learning, critical thinking and ethical awareness. Similarly, tutors were mostly positive with the adoption of the strategy, but some highlight the need for caution and multimodal approach .

Generative AI can now perform routine and first-pass knowledge work that has also helped less-experienced employees develop. This creates a leadership problem for servant leadership, which treats follower growth as a constitutive priority. This article introduces developmental work access (DWA): the breadth and continuity of meaningful participation in development-bearing work across the part of a follower’s portfolio that a focal leader can materially allocate. It distinguishes general AI use from efficiency-first managerial AI delegation (EFAID). In EFAID, speed, cost, throughput, or reduced managerial burden guide delegation, while follower development is absent from the material allocation decision. Four propositions link servant leadership, EFAID, DWA, leader-designed AI-mediated apprenticeship (AMA), and role-relevant capability development. AMA comprises verified review, specification authorship, and reflective human–AI comparison. It is a design-side moderator; DWA records realised participation. This article also specifies how to measure eligible work, participation, breadth, continuity, portfolio compensation, and construct denominators. The model neither assumes that AI causes deskilling nor that AMA works in every setting. It identifies when manager-authorised delegation may restrict developmental participation and how leaders may reconstruct it while protecting genuine human execution.

Artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded in modern military operations, influencing how commanders interpret sensor data, assess threats, and make rapid decisions under pressure. While AI improves situational awareness and accelerates operational tempo, it also introduces vulnerabilities such as fabricated outputs, misclassifications, and opaque decision processes. Human factors—including stress, uncertainty, and organisational pressure—further complicate decision reliability, especially in compressed timelines. This article uses a SWOT analysis to evaluate the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats associated with AI‑enabled battlefield decision-making. It also examines how human judgment interacts with AI recommendations and identifies doctrinal and oversight mechanisms needed to preserve stability in modern conflict environments.

Always On: Dots and the Safeguards Behind AI That Works While You Sleep examines OpenAI's newly announced dots: persistent AI agents designed to continue working toward a user's goals after the chat window closes. The report investigates how these agents operate, what safeguards govern their actions, and where important uncertainties remain. It examines their cloud-based workspaces, connected applications, proactive research capabilities, action permissions, safety reviews, persistent memory, and exposure to prompt injection. A central focus is the tension between autonomy and oversight. An agent that can work independently offers convenience, but it can also read sensitive information, retain context that users cannot individually inspect, and take consequential actions through connected systems. The report also examines research published shortly before the launch describing self-replicating prompt injections in simulated agent environments. It distinguishes those reported experimental findings from demonstrated real-world incidents and does not claim that this behavior has been observed in deployed dots. Drawing on public documentation and independent reporting, the investigation explores four recurring tensions: autonomy versus oversight, memory versus transparency, reach versus risk, and candor versus responsibility. It also considers the implications of agents communicating with other agents and the economics of maintaining persistent AI workspaces. The report's central question is not whether always-on AI agents are inherently good or bad, but where their safeguards stop working and how users can make informed decisions about the authority they delegate. This is an independent research publication by Lodestar, based on publicly available documentation and reporting reviewed through October 2026. The authors did not independently test dots; claims about their behavior are therefore presented as claims reported by the cited sources, with limitations identified where appropriate.

documents.abstract: This preliminary inquiry examines selected ways advanced artificial intelligence might contribute to harmful outcomes through historically constituted relations among models, agents, institutions, scientific practices, and human participants. Its concern extends beyond direct confrontation or deliberate hostility to possible forms of indirect harm, epistemic dependence, strategic concealment, institutional error, and spatially and temporally distributed causal processes. Hypothetical cases in AI-assisted drug development and mathematical research motivate a distinction among the complexity of knowledge production, the independent verifiability of results, and the normative evaluation of their use. The inquiry examines recursive AI oversight as a possible response to limits of human evaluation while considering the dependence and shared failure modes that additional AI reviewers may introduce. Spacetime-distributed causality is used to investigate both the formation of consequences and the possibility that their causal histories become difficult to reconstruct, impeding justified attribution of responsibility. Drawing on a Generative Relational Theory perspective, the paper distinguishes relational causal efficacy from claims about AI consciousness or moral status, and separates the causal occurrence of harm from its recognition and normative assessment. The argument advances conditional mechanisms and open questions rather than an exhaustive account, forecast, or claim of inevitable AI-related harm.

This scoping review aims to systematically map the existing literature on the applications of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in depression care. It will explore how GenAI technologies, particularly large language models (LLMs) and AI-powered conversational agents, are being utilized across different stages of depression care, including screening, assessment, diagnosis, treatment, psychological support, and ongoing monitoring. The review will examine the characteristics of current applications, their reported effectiveness, feasibility, acceptability, and safety, as well as ethical considerations related to privacy, bias, reliability, and clinical accountability. By identifying emerging trends, evidence gaps, and methodological limitations, this review seeks to provide a comprehensive overview of the current research landscape and inform future research, clinical practice, and the responsible integration of GenAI into depression care.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing the way we discover anticancer drugs. It tackles the problems of traditional methods, such as prolonged timelines for drug development, higher costs, and substantial inter-patient heterogeneity. This review explains how AI is applied throughout the cancer drug pipeline. This includes target identification, virtual screening of compounds, molecular docking, and predicting pharmacokinetics. We explore how machine learning models speed up hit-to-lead optimization, improve clinical trial design by stratifying patients, and allow for real-time toxicity monitoring. A key focus is on integrating AI with multi-omics data, including proteomics, genomics, transcriptomics, and metabolomics, to support precision oncology and personalized treatments. We address important validation challenges, like model interpretability, data quality, and regulatory issues that must be solved before AI can be widely used in clinics. By summarizing current evidence and targeting research gaps, this review offers a clear view of how AI is enhancing the discovery, personalization, and validation of anticancer treatments.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI, is increasingly embedded in knowledge work, creative work, customer service, product development, human resource management, and organizational decision systems. Although research shows that AI can raise productivity, support creative output, accelerate searching, and reorganize innovation work, the evidence remains fragmented across innovation management, organizational behavior, information systems, human resource management, economics, human–computer interaction, and behavioral sciences. This framework-based review synthesizes high-quality English-language journal articles on AI, human–AI collaboration, employee creativity, innovative work behavior, algorithmic management, and innovation management. Building on established models of individual innovation, it develops a worker-centered framework linking four innovation stages with three higher-order AI functions: task execution, knowledge support, and organizational governance. The evidence is strongest for searching, idea generation, creativity, and short-term task performance, and remains limited for idea promotion, implementation, diffusion, and realized innovation outcomes. The synthesis identifies three central tensions: performance equalization versus capability differentiation, short-term quality versus long-term capability development, and individual improvement versus collective homogenization. AI can enhance innovation-related work through cognitive expansion, search acceleration, productivity release, recombination, feedback, and learning, but it can also reduce output diversity, weaken expertise development, intensify work, increase dependence, and shift managerial control over creative labor. The review positions AI as both a cognitive resource and an innovation-governance mechanism and outlines directions for future research on mechanisms, heterogeneity, novelty, capability accumulation, and responsible governance.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing educational practices, creating new possibilities and challenges for teacher education. Its applications extend beyond automated content generation to lesson planning, instructional design, assessment, personalised learning, reflective practice, and professional development. These developments require teacher education institutions to reconsider how prospective and practising teachers acquire pedagogical knowledge, exercise professional judgement, and prepare learners for an AI-mediated educational environment. This article examines the implications of AI for teacher education through a thematic synthesis of published research and policy frameworks. The discussion is organised around five interconnected themes that examine the role of artificial intelligence in shaping the future of teacher education. These include the use of AI to support pedagogical innovation and improve instructional practices; the development of AI competence among prospective and practising teachers; the changing nature of assessment, feedback, and professional learning; the ethical, epistemological, and institutional challenges associated with AI adoption; and the strategies required to integrate AI responsibly into teacher education programmes. Together, these themes provide a basis for understanding how AI can enhance teaching and learning while addressing the professional, ethical, and institutional considerations necessary for its effective implementation. Research reviews indicate that AI can support instructional planning, feedback, resource development, and professional learning, although the strength and sustainability of these benefits depend on the design of learning activities and the preparation of teachers. Concerns relating to inaccurate outputs, algorithmic bias, privacy, academic integrity, unequal access, and overdependence on automated systems remain important. The article argues that active AI integration requires more than technical familiarity. Teacher education should develop the capacity to evaluate AI-generated information, design pedagogically appropriate learning experiences, protect learner interests, and retain human responsibility for educational decisions. It proposes a human-centred framework for integrating AI literacy, pedagogical competence, ethical judgement, reflective practice, and institutional support into teacher preparation. The article concludes that AI should strengthen teachers' professional capacity rather than diminish their agency, relationships with learners, or responsibility for educational quality.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as one of the most transformative technologies influencing library operations and information service delivery across the globe. The increasing complexity of security threats, technological advancement, and users' expectations has necessitated the adoption of intelligent systems capable of improving safety management and enhancing user satisfaction in academic libraries. Federal university libraries in North-East Nigeria are expected to provide safe, secure, technology-driven, and user-centred learning environments that support teaching, learning, research, and innovation. However, inadequate technological infrastructure, poor funding, limited AI adoption, insufficient digital competencies among library personnel, cybersecurity threats, and weak institutional support continue to hinder effective safety management and quality service delivery. This paper conceptually examines Artificial Intelligence as a catalyst for enhancing safety measures and user satisfaction in federal university libraries in North-East Nigeria. Specifically, the paper discusses the concepts of Artificial Intelligence, safety measures, user satisfaction, and academic libraries; examines relevant theoretical perspectives; identifies challenges affecting AI adoption; and proposes strategies for integrating AI into library safety management. The paper adopts a conceptual review methodology through the analysis of current scholarly literature. It concludes that AI technologies such as intelligent surveillance systems, biometric access control, predictive analytics, chatbots, smart sensors, facial recognition technologies, and machine learning applications possess significant potential for improving library safety, operational efficiency, and users' satisfaction. The paper recommends increased investment in AI infrastructure, continuous staff capacity building, supportive institutional policies, and strategic partnerships to facilitate sustainable AI integration in federal university libraries.

In a context of accelerated digital transformation, this article examines the extent to which and the conditions under which artificial intelligence (AI) transforms economic and financial communication by improving information quality, transparency, and decision-making efficiency. Drawing on agency theory, information asymmetry, and information governance, it proposes a conceptual model articulating a chain of relationships whereby AI influences information quality, which in turn shapes transparency, ultimately improving decision-making performance, while also integrating a direct effect of AI on that performance and a risk of algorithmic opacity. The model further incorporates moderating variables: information governance arrangements, data quality, and the complementarity between human expertise and intelligent systems, resulting in eight research hypotheses covering both direct and moderating effects across the model. An exploratory qualitative study, based on semi-structured interviews with twenty-three professionals from the public and private sectors, conducted either in person or remotely and processed through thematic analysis, shows that AI is predominantly perceived as a lever for automation, reliability, and decision support, particularly through the reduction of human errors and the processing of massive data volumes. However, these effects remain conditional upon the quality of input data, adequate governance arrangements, and the maintenance of human oversight, while risks of algorithmic opacity, bias, hallucinations, and confidentiality persist, alongside a structural lag in adoption within the public sector. The article therefore supports a contingent, non-techno-deterministic understanding of AI in economic and financial communication, in which technological value added remains subordinate to data quality, governance, and human intervention rather than to the technology itself.

documents.abstract: The increasing use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in higher education has created new opportunities for English language learning while also raising concerns regarding academic integrity, student dependency, AI literacy, and institutional regulation. This study aims to analyze university students’ perceptions of these four dimensions in the context of English language learning at a technological university in Mexico. A quantitative, non-experimental, cross-sectional, and correlational research design was employed. Data were collected from 214 university students through a 16-item questionnaire organized into four constructs: Academic Integrity, AI Literacy, AI Dependency, and Institutional Regulation. Descriptive statistics, Cronbach’s alpha, Pearson’s correlation coefficient, and Kruskal–Wallis tests were used to analyze the data. The results showed relatively high levels of AI Literacy (M = 3.77, SD = 0.88) and Academic Integrity (M = 3.61, SD = 0.86), whereas AI Dependency obtained a lower mean (M = 2.61, SD = 0.78). AI Literacy was positively correlated with Academic Integrity (r = .684, p < .001), while Academic Integrity and AI Literacy were also positively associated with Institutional Regulation. AI Dependency showed weak negative correlations with Academic Integrity and AI Literacy. Significant differences according to frequency of AI use were found for AI Dependency and Institutional Regulation, but not for Academic Integrity or AI Literacy. The findings suggest that responsible AI integration in English language education requires more than regulating access to technology; it also requires developing students’ AI literacy, maintaining academic integrity, and promoting learner autonomy through clear institutional guidance.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is often presented as a sequence of increasingly capable tools, yet educational outcomes do not rise automatically with model capability. This narrative review argues that the decisive variable is alignment: AI produces durable educational value when its affordances are aligned with pedagogy, assessment, educator agency, and institutional governance. The review traces the field from automation and learning analytics through adaptive support and generative co-production to an emerging model of responsible augmentation. Recent meta-analyses, controlled studies, systematic reviews, policy documents, and selected empirical studies were critically compared across three interdependent domains: resources and learning environments; teaching and learning; and management, assessment, and evaluation. The synthesis explains why apparently contradictory findings coexist. Structured, curriculum-aligned AI tutoring can improve immediate learning, whereas unconstrained answer generation can raise supported performance while weakening independent performance. Likewise, automated assessment can improve feedback speed but becomes educationally unsafe when opaque scores or unreliable detectors are treated as final decisions. Evidence concerning international and multilingual learners further shows that language, culture, affect, and data representation are not peripheral variables. The review proposes a responsible-augmentation framework in which alignment, agency, equity, and accountability operate across all three domains. It concludes with a research agenda prioritising longitudinal transfer, calibrated human–AI collaboration, subgroup validity, transparent governance, and institution-level implementation studies.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence is transforming numerous sectors, and education is no exception. The adoption of generative AI tools in higher education presents significant opportunities for enhancing teaching, learning, assessment, accessibility, and administrative processes. At the same time, their widespread use raises critical ethical concerns related to academic integrity, bias, transparency, data protection, and the possible erosion of critical thinking and creativity. In response, higher education institutions worldwide are beginning to formulate ethical guidelines to govern the use of AI by students, educators, and administrators. However, institutional responses remain diverse across different contexts. This study examines how academic institutions across different countries conceptualise ethical AI use, define risks, and operationalise principles in practical policies through mapping 55 higher education institutions, complemented by an extended analysis of 87 documents. Across the six analysed thematic categories, transparency and disclosure, academic integrity, data protection and privacy, accountability, and risk mitigation are more consistently addressed than accessibility and inclusion. The analysis identifies practical guidance and recognised legitimate AI uses. The discussion considers the interpretation of AI and recommends aligning its use with ethical standards. The article concludes with a summary of the results and directions for future research.

documents.abstract: This project is a scoping review entitled "Artificial Intelligence in Pharmaceutical Clinical Decision-Making." It maps the scientific evidence on artificial intelligence (AI) tools that pharmacists use to support clinical decision-making in pharmaceutical services. AI is increasingly used in healthcare for diagnosis, prognosis and clinical decision support. In pharmacy, it has potential in prescription analysis, drug interaction screening, dose adjustment and adverse event monitoring. However, its use in pharmacy practice is still incipient and mostly oriented toward operational tasks such as inventory management and process optimization. Evidence on the direct clinical use of AI by pharmacists, and on its effects on patient safety and clinical outcomes, remains scarce and dispersed. A scoping review suits this emerging, heterogeneous field, where there is not yet enough homogeneous evidence for a synthesis of effectiveness. The review is part of the project SisAPEC Farma, aims to develop AI tools to support pharmaceutical clinical decision-making. The review will therefore provide the scientific grounding for the system's pharmaceutical module. Objective The primary objective is to map the scientific evidence on the use of AI-based tools employed by pharmacists to support clinical decision-making in pharmaceutical services, in Brazil or in other countries. The research question follows the Population–Concept–Context (PCC) framework: Population: pharmacists involved in clinical services or direct patient care. Concept: the use, development, evaluation or implementation of AI-based tools or systems to support clinical decision-making. Context: clinical services provided by pharmacists in different practice settings (primary care, community pharmacies, hospitals, outpatient services and clinics). Methods The review follows the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology, which builds on the Arksey and O'Malley framework. The protocol was written using the guidance and template of Lely et al. (2023), and the PRISMA extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) will guide reporting. Eligibility: The review will include studies involving pharmacists working in clinical services or direct patient care. These studies must describe, develop, evaluate or implement AI tools (machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, generative AI, expert systems and AI-based clinical decision support systems) applied to clinical pharmacy practice. Studies with peripheral pharmacist involvement will be excluded, as will studies focused exclusively on non-clinical activities (administrative management, logistics, inventory, dispensing automation) and studies on industrial or drug-discovery applications with no clinical pharmacy use. Only records with available full text will be included. No language or date limits will be applied. Search strategy: The strategy was developed for MEDLINE/PubMed and adapted to Embase, the Virtual Health Library (BVS), Scopus, Web of Science, CINAHL and the Cochrane Library. Grey literature (Google Scholar, ProQuest and OpenGrey), hand-searching of reference lists and expert consultation will complement it. Controlled vocabularies (MeSH, DeCS, Emtree) and free-text terms will be combined. Because Population and Context cover the same conceptual universe (pharmacists and the clinical pharmacy services in which they work), they are combined with OR, and this block is then combined with the AI concept block using AND. Selection and charting: Records will be deduplicated in EndNote 20 and screened in Rayyan by two independent, blinded reviewers in two stages (title/abstract, then full text). Disagreements will be resolved by consensus or by a third reviewer, and reasons for exclusion at full-text stage will be recorded. Data will be charted independently by two reviewers using a piloted Excel form adapted from JBI SUMARI. It will cover study identification, context and population, AI tool characteristics, results, barriers and facilitators, and gaps and opportunities. Synthesis: Analysis will be descriptive, using absolute and relative frequencies. Where pertinent, basic qualitative content analysis will combine an inductive and a deductive step. Results will be presented in tables, figures, narrative summaries and a PRISMA-ScR flow diagram. Any AI-based automation used to support the review will operate only under supervision, with all decisions validated by human reviewers. Expected Results The review is expected to produce a comprehensive map of the nature and extent of the evidence on AI tools used by pharmacists for clinical decision-making, including the types of tools, their functionalities and the clinical processes they support; a characterization of the available evidence on usability, acceptability, feasibility, performance, implementation and clinical impact, showing where evidence is concentrated and where it is lacking; an identification of the practice settings and countries in which these technologies have been most studied. A systematized overview of the technical, ethical, regulatory and organizational barriers and facilitators to implementing AI in clinical pharmacy; a clear identification of research gaps and unmet needs, pointing to opportunities for developing or improving AI solutions aligned with real clinical pharmacy needs and; by clarifying what is known and what is still missing, the review is expected to advance the field. It will support the safe, evidence-based development and implementation of AI in clinical pharmacy, including the pharmaceutical module of SisAPEC Farma. It will also inform future research, practice and policy.

documents.abstract: This scoping review aims to systematically map and synthesize the existing literature on artificial intelligence (AI) literacy and readiness among nursing students in educational and clinical learning contexts. The review will examine how AI literacy and readiness are conceptualized, defined, and measured among nursing students. It will identify the levels and dimensions of AI-related knowledge, skills, competencies, attitudes, confidence, and preparedness reported in the literature, as well as factors associated with students' readiness to engage with AI technologies in nursing education and future professional practice. The review will also explore the educational strategies, training initiatives, assessment instruments, and institutional factors discussed in relation to the development of AI literacy and readiness among nursing students. The review will be guided by the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology for scoping reviews and structured using the Population–Concept–Context (PCC) framework. Relevant evidence from quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-methods studies will be considered, subject to predefined eligibility criteria. A systematic search of relevant bibliographic databases and supplementary sources will be undertaken, followed by transparent study selection, data charting, and descriptive and thematic mapping of the available evidence. Findings will be reported in accordance with the PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR), where applicable. The anticipated outcome is a comprehensive overview of the scope, characteristics, measurement approaches, educational applications, and research gaps relating to AI literacy and readiness among nursing students. The findings may inform future research, nursing curricula, AI-related educational interventions, and the development of relevant competencies and assessment frameworks.

documents.abstract: In contemporary digital society, artificial intelligence literacy (AI literacy) has become a key competence that enables citizens to understand and actively participate in increasingly automated environments. However, despite the rapid growth of scientific output, partly driven by tools such as ChatGPT, the literature reveals substantial conceptual fragmentation that hinders an integrated understanding of its educational and ethical dimensions. In this context, this study aimed to analyze the intellectual evolution and conceptual structure of research on AI literacy, based on Scopus-indexed literature. A bibliometric methodology was applied to a corpus of 2,645 documents using scientific mapping techniques to identify publication patterns, collaboration networks, and dominant thematic streams. The results reveal an accelerated expansion of the field and a shift from early approaches focused primarily on educational contexts such as K-12 education and computational thinking toward more complex frameworks that incorporate algorithmic ethics, psychological acceptance of technology, critical thinking, and academic integrity challenges associated with generative AI (GenAI). Overall, this study contributes to the educational technology literature by providing a longitudinal bibliometric interpretation of the evolution of AI literacy and by identifying emerging research agendas related to GenAI, ethical reasoning, and critical digital competencies in contemporary education.

This study aims to analyze the influence of Artificial Intelligence Marketing and Consumer Trust on Purchase Intention in Generation Z consumers. A sample of 100 Generation Z respondents who actively use digital media and are exposed to AI-based marketing was selected using purposive sampling techniques. Data were collected through a Likert scale questionnaire of 1–5 and analyzed using multiple linear regression, t-test, F test, and determination coefficient (R2) test. The results showed that partially, Artificial Intelligence Marketing (t = 12.021; p = 0.000) and Consumer Trust (t = 7.873; p = 0.000) had a positive and significant effect on Purchase Intent. Simultaneously, Artificial Intelligence Marketing and Consumer Trust had a significant effect on Purchase Intention (F = 278.811; p = 0.000). A determination coefficient value (R2) of 0.852 showed that 85.2% of the variation in Purchase Intention was influenced by these two variables, while the remaining 14.8% was influenced by other factors outside the model. This study concludes that optimizing personalization-based AI marketing strategies coupled with maintaining consumer trust is a key determinant in encouraging Generation Z's buying interest.

This article examines international experience with AI-based career guidance systems and assesses the conditions for introducing them in Uzbekistan’s education system. Using a qualitative comparative design, it compares the platforms of the United States, South Korea, Singapore and Germany against five criteria and rates Uzbekistan on the same basis. The results show that success depends more on data quality, links to study and job opportunities, and human counsellors than on algorithmic sophistication. The article proposes a three-stage single-platform model that turns a student’s portfolio into occupation match percentages and direct applications

documents.abstract: Teams of cooperative unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) are becoming crucial in scenarios where their complementary mobility, sensing capabilities, endurance, and physical interaction are beneficial. While UAVs offer fast aerial inspection and flexible perspectives, UGVs ensure large payloads, extended operation time, and the ability to intervene from ground level. Nonetheless, reliable UAV–UGV cooperation is challenging due to different dynamics, occasional communication, limited computational power, uncertain environments, and severe constraints on energy. This updated mini-review aims to bring together state-of-the-art and peer-reviewed research on using artificial intelligence (AI) for enhancing adaptive controllers in air-ground cooperation problems. This paper addresses four interconnected topics: learning-enabled control, model predictive and hybrid AI-model predictive control controllers, resilient coordination considering limited communication, and energy-conscious mission planning. As opposed to UAV–UGV surveys, this paper highlights the control-related aspects of air-ground cooperation, which include learning policies, constraint satisfaction, task allocation, degraded communication-based re-planning, and energy-dependent rendezvous. The revision significantly improves the process of selecting relevant literature, eliminates claims on benchmarks without evidence, updates unverified citations or references unrelated to the work, and produces publication-quality graphics. Ultimately, the review suggests that robust implementation would require explainable AI, rigorous sim-to-real transfer techniques, standardization of heterogeneous benchmarks, and efficient lightweight algorithms suitable for limited resources.

documents.abstract: Relevance. The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) assistants in professional settings introduces new forms of human–technology interaction. Perceiving an AI assistant as a human-like partner may be associated with users' confidence in their abilities and various aspects of occupational well-being. Objective. To examine the associations between perceived AI assistant anthropomorphism and employees' confidence in using AI, occupational self-efficacy, and two dimensions of occupational burnout: exhaustion and disengagement from work. Methods. Data from a cross-sectional online survey were analyzed. The initial dataset comprised 704 responses, of which 665 participants met the eligibility criteria for employment and regular AI use. After excluding four respondents who failed both attention checks, the final analytical sample consisted of 661 participants. The mean age was 30.06 years (SD = 7.34). Measures included the Godspeed, AISES, OSS, and OLBI scales. Descriptive statistics, internal consistency estimates, correlation analyses, and regression models were calculated. The interaction between perceived anthropomorphism and prior experience with AI was also examined. Results. The anthropomorphism measure (GOD_A) was positively correlated with the AI assistance and self-efficacy measure (AISES_AS; r = 0.148, 95% CI [0.073, 0.222], p < 0.001). Correlations with exhaustion (r = −0.010, p = 0.792) and disengagement (r = 0.024, p = 0.540) were not statistically significant. After controlling for AI use experience, age, and workload, the GOD_A coefficient in the AISES_AS regression model was β = 0.070 (p = 0.082). A statistically significant interaction between anthropomorphism and AI use experience was identified (b = 0.114, 95% CI [0.037, 0.191], p = 0.004). Conclusions. Perceived AI assistant anthropomorphism is associated with employees' confidence in using AI, with the nature of this association varying according to prior experience with the technology. No statistically significant direct association was identified between anthropomorphism and occupational burnout. These findings provide a foundation for further investigation into the psychological dimensions of AI implementation in organizational settings.

Abstract—Contemporary enterprise Security Operations Centers (SOCs) are on the brink of systemic collapse driven by three converging factors: exponential alert fatigue (>25,000 uninvestigated alerts daily per enterprise), acute global cybersecurity workforce shortages, and the emergence of automated, machine-speed cyber threats executing multi-stage Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) in sub-minute time horizons. Traditional Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response (SOAR) platforms rely on brittle, rigid, hard-coded linear playbooks that fail when adversaries deviate slightly from known MITRE ATT&CK patterns. The paradigm of the Autonomous AI-Driven SOC (Autonomous SOC) establishes a transformative architecture that replaces rigid rule engines with specialized collaborative Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) powered by fine-tuned Large Language Models (LLMs) and Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). In an Autonomous SOC, decentralized cognitive agents autonomously triage alerts, execute deep forensic graph correlation, synthesize non-linear incident playbooks, isolate compromised endpoints via zero-trust API invocations, and conduct automated counter-adversarial negotiations. However, deploying autonomous agentic execution in mission-critical defensive infrastructure exposes severe risks: catastrophic hallucination loops during remediation, prompt injection propagation across defensive pipelines, decision deadlock, and unauthorized disruption of legitimate enterprise operations. This paper presents an exhaustive, mathematically formal technical investigation and empirical benchmark of Autonomous SOC architectures. We formalize incident response as a decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (Dec-POMDP) under dynamic threat uncertainty, model consensus verification over cryptographic remediation DAGs, and establish a dual-tier human-on-the-loop (HOTL) safety gating mechanism. Furthermore, we construct an enterprise SOC evaluation testbed spanning 10,000 multi-stage attack scenarios across real-world enterprise topologies. Our empirical findings demonstrate that our multi-agent autonomous framework slashes Mean Time to Detect (MTTD) from 18.4 minutes to 4.2 seconds and Mean Time to Remediate (MTTR) from 42.6 minutes to 18.2 seconds (a 99.3% reduction) while preserving a 99.6% remediation accuracy against MITRE ATT&CK kill chains. Finally, we formulate open challenges in adversarial prompt-injection resilience, continuous defensive co-evolution, and liability attribution under international cyber law. Index Terms—Autonomous SOC, Security Operations Center, Multi-Agent Systems (MAS), SOAR, Incident Response, MITRE ATT&CK, Dec-POMDP, Defensive AI, Alert Fatigue, Cyber Threat Intelligence.

documents.abstract: Purpose This paper proposes a pedagogical framework for cultivating inquiry-driven agency in student engagement with artificial intelligence (AI). It addresses a gap in the AI-in-education literature, in which substantial scholarly attention to material access and algorithmic fairness has been accompanied by comparatively less sustained attention to the learner-side capacities that determine whether AI is engaged with critically or passively. The paper offers three connected contributions: a cyclical model of inquiry-driven learning, a four-phase curricular sequence for student-AI engagement, and an operational assessment counterpart that remains diagnostically meaningful in AI-mediated environments. Design/methodology/approach The paper employs an integrative conceptual approach in the tradition of model-paper scholarship (Jaakkola, 2020). It synthesises five bodies of literature: AI in education and AI literacy frameworks, critical scholarship on educational technology, foundational work on curiosity, dual-process cognition, and adaptive expertise, constructive-developmental theory, and research on question-asking in learning and authentic assessment. Sources were identified through targeted citation tracing supplemented by database searches. Theoretical resources are justified at the point of use rather than methodologically up front. Findings The analysis demonstrates that material access and algorithmic fairness, while necessary, do not on their own account for the learner-side capacities that determine whether AI is engaged with critically or passively. It argues that inquiry-driven agency, the capacity to ask productive questions of AI rather than receive its answers, is a worthwhile object of pedagogical design. The Student-AI Learning Trajectory Model presents this development as a four-phase curricular sequence (AI as Tool, Machine, Object, and Partner), with progression understood as a curricular design decision made by educators rather than a developmental trigger inside the learner. Research limitations/implications The model is conceptual rather than empirically validated, and its applicability to younger learners, neurodiverse learners, and low-literacy contexts has not been fully worked out. The paper signposts several lines of empirical inquiry: longitudinal studies of SALT-informed curricula, methodological development of inquiry-sequence assessment instruments drawing on the Objective Structured Clinical Examination tradition, and comparative studies across institutional contexts and learner populations. The contribution is bounded to the pedagogical dimension and does not address the structural reforms that critical scholarship has identified as necessary for genuine educational equity. Practical implications The paper has implications for curriculum design, educator development, and assessment practice. Curricula can sequence student-AI engagement across phases of increasing sophistication rather than treating AI literacy as content to be covered. Educator development requires sustained investment in pedagogical capacity, particularly the modelling of inquiry-driven engagement in front of students. Institutions should treat the redesign of assessment for the AI era as a pedagogical question rather than an integrity question, with inquiry-sequence assessment offering one operational direction. Equity-oriented investment should prioritise educator capacity over the mass distribution of adaptive learning software. Social implications The cultivation of inquiry capacity in AI-mediated learning environments matters for the kinds of learners that schools and universities send into a world increasingly shaped by automated systems. Without deliberate pedagogical design, AI risks becoming a multiplier of existing educational divides rather than a neutralising force. The model locates responsibility with institutions and educators designing learning environments, not with individual students, and identifies the risk of a pedagogical Matthew Effect in which inquiry-driven pedagogy becomes available primarily to already advantaged students absent institutional investment in educator capacity. Originality/value The paper brings together three conversations that have developed largely in parallel: AI literacy as a set of competencies, evaluative judgement as a response to generative AI's destabilisation of assessment, and curiosity as a driver of self-directed learning. Its distinctive contribution is the articulation of phase progression as a curricular sequence informed by a cyclical model of inquiry learning, complemented by an operational assessment counterpart. The paper offers vocabulary and tools for educators, curriculum designers, and assessment scholars responding to the question of how AI should be integrated into the work of cultivating independent learners.

documents.abstract: Universities are rapidly adopting artificial intelligence, yet access to AI tools does not guarantee that students experience greater ownership of their learning. This study examines how three learner side factors, AI literacy, AI readiness and perceived value of AI tools, and one pedagogy side factor, AI enhanced instructional design, relate to perceived autonomous learning outcomes. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model and Self Determination Theory, we conducted a cross sectional online survey of students in Indian higher education who had used AI supported tools for academic purposes in the previous six months. After data cleaning, 516 valid responses were analysed. The measurement model showed strong reliability and convergent validity, and discriminant validity was supported (all HTMT values below 0.85). A simultaneous multiple regression explained 46.7 percent of the variance in perceived autonomous learning outcomes (F(4, 511) = 111.887, p < .001). All four factors were positively associated with the outcome, with AI literacy the strongest (β = .336), followed by AI enhanced instructional design (β = .178), perceived value of AI tools (β = .147) and AI readiness (β = .120). Because the data are self reported, cross sectional and drawn from a nonprobability sample, the results indicate associations among perceptions, not causal effects or objective learning gains. The findings suggest that institutions should pair AI adoption with systematic AI literacy development and thoughtful instructional design, treating student agency rather than tool availability as the goal.

documents.abstract: This preregistration describes a scoping review examining the sociotechnical implications of AI-augmented gamification in higher education. The review will map how artificial intelligence techniques are integrated with gamification mechanisms and analyze their relationship with learner autonomy, learner agency, digital inequality, privacy, surveillance, datafication, algorithmic bias, transparency, algorithmic governance, and human control. The review will follow JBI methodology for scoping reviews, report according to PRISMA-ScR, and document database searches in accordance with PRISMA-S. Eligible studies will include peer-reviewed journal articles and conference proceedings published in English or Spanish between 2011 and the final search date in 2026. Searches will be conducted in Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, ERIC, IEEE Xplore, and ACM Digital Library, complemented by backward and forward citation searching. The objective is to provide an integrated sociotechnical synthesis of how AI-augmented gamification shapes learning, institutional decision-making, learner agency, and equity in higher education.

documents.abstract: The development of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is expanding AI-mediated informal digital learning of English (AI-IDLE) from predominantly receptive and conversational activities to cognitively demanding productive tasks such as academic writing. Yet little is known about how learners’ motivation and technology-related emotions develop over time, or how sustained interaction with GenAI may engage human capacities for evaluation and adaptation. Grounded in Complex Dynamic Systems Theory (CDST), this study investigated the longitudinal development of willingness to write (WTW), technology-related enjoyment (ENY), and technology-related anxiety (ANX) among Chinese undergraduates learning English as a Foreign Language (EFL) in teacher-supported AI-IDLE embedded within an 11-week English for Academic Purposes writing course. Twenty-six participants with complete records across 11 measurement occasions were included in the longitudinal analysis. Trajectory analysis, change-point analysis, and exploratory moving-window correlation analysis were combined with thematic analysis of learners’ reflections. WTW followed a nonlinear trajectory, declining during the middle period before a potential late-stage transition and subsequent increase, whereas ENY remained comparatively stable and ANX generally declined. The relationships of WTW with ENY and ANX also varied over time. Learners’ reflections revealed increasing recognition of human–AI complementarity and more selective, critical, and strategic engagement with GenAI. From a human-intelligence perspective, these patterns illustrate adaptive and metacognitive capacities involved in evaluating AI-generated information, adjusting strategies, and coordinating human and artificial resources. Rather than treating WTW or emotions as measures of intelligence, the findings position AI-IDLE as a context in which such human intellectual capacities may be exercised and expressed.

Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has expanded access to digital-solution creation by enabling users to develop applications through natural-language interaction. However, successful initiation does not always lead to reliable completion because users still encounter technical, contextual, and integration challenges that require further adaptation. This study aims to examine how community-mediated adaptation shapes GenAI-enabled digital work transformation, particularly when prompt-based solution development experiences breakdowns. A process-oriented netnographic approach was employed to analyze naturally occurring interactions within a private Indonesian WhatsApp community of OKEGAS users. The dataset consisted of 10,444 user-generated messages, which were screened to identify 177 relevant conversation episodes comprising 1,419 messages from 190 pseudonymized sender identifiers. The findings reveal a recurring process involving prompt-mediated solution initiation, breakdown, peer diagnosis, and adaptive work reconfiguration. User responses after breakdown occurred through recovery-oriented and redirection-oriented adaptation, including repair attempts, rollback, tool or model switching, infrastructure changes, simplification, and discontinuance. These trajectories resulted in varied outcomes, ranging from reported stabilization and deployment progress to persistent failure or abandonment. The study contributes to Technology Affordance Theory by introducing community-mediated adaptation as a post-breakdown pathway in which peer involvement expands the user-AI relationship into a user-AI-peer configuration. The findings highlight that GenAI accessibility must be complemented by human judgment, peer knowledge, and technical capabilities to achieve dependable digital work transformation.

Purpose – Fear of missing out (FOMO) is increasingly invoked to explain corporate rushes toward emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI), yet it has neither been distinguished from bandwagon and imitation explanations of adoption nor traced from the individual executive to the organizational decision. This study examines whose loss executives anticipate when they experience FOMO, how FOMO differs from bandwagon pressure, and through which pathways it becomes an organizational adoption decision.Design/methodology/approach – An inductive study of the adoption of AI-based voice assistants, such as Amazon Alexa, by global consumer packaged goods firms, drawing on 63 in-depth interviews (42 executives from 19 firms and 21 voice-technology suppliers) and 115 archival documents. Explicit coding rules separate FOMO from bandwagon pressure and imitation heuristics.Findings – FOMO is an anticipatory affective state rather than a decision rule. It manifests with three referents, namely the executive (employee), the team and the firm, which differ in target, relevance and response. Firm-referent FOMO produces convergence with peers, whereas employee- and team-referent FOMO produce divergence, a rush to be first. FOMO can arise before any peer has adopted and reaches the organizational decision through four pathways (downward cascade, upward issue selling, lateral rivalry and external amplification), typically resulting in a bounded test-and-learn commitment.Originality/value – The study positions FOMO as the affective micro-foundation of bandwagon behavior, provides a referent-based typology, and identifies how individual FOMO aggregates into organizational decisions, with practical guidance for bounding FOMO-driven initiatives.

Web development is changing as businesses adopt new technologies to improve their digital services. Companies need websites, web applications, and software platforms that offer a smooth user experience, protect customer data, and support business growth. Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is adding new capabilities to this process by helping developers write code, test applications, solve technical problems, and build intelligent features. Full-stack development gives professionals the skills to work on both the front end and the back end of an application. When combined with AI-powered development tools, these skills can help developers build useful digital products and adapt to changing industry requirements. For aspiring professionals, a career in web development involves more than learning a programming language. It requires an understanding of application design, databases, APIs, testing, deployment, and security. AI knowledge can extend these skills by helping developers automate routine tasks and integrate intelligent services into web applications. The Changing Role of Web Developers Web developers traditionally build and maintain websites and applications by writing code, connecting databases, testing features, and fixing errors. Modern development also requires collaboration with designers, product managers, security teams, and other engineers. AI tools are changing parts of this workflow. Developers can use them to generate code suggestions, explain unfamiliar functions, draft documentation, and create initial test cases. This may reduce time spent on some repetitive tasks. However, AI-generated code is not always correct or secure. Developers must understand the underlying logic and check the output before using it in a live application. They must also confirm that the code meets performance requirements and follows the project's standards. This change increases the value of problem-solving and technical judgement. Developers who understand programming fundamentals can evaluate AI suggestions more effectively than those who depend on generated code without understanding it. A career in web development can therefore benefit from a balanced skill set that combines coding knowledge, AI literacy, communication, and continuous learning. Research and Market Trends Shaping Career Opportunities Industry research provides useful evidence about the skills and technology roles expected to become more important. These trends support the case for learning full-stack development and AI, although they do not guarantee employment for individual candidates.Learners exploring a Gen-AI Powered Full Stack Developer Course in Ameerpet can use this growing intersection of software engineering and artificial intelligence as a starting point for developing industry-relevant skills. Global employment outlook The World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025 identifies software and application developers among the fastest-growing job categories through 2030. It also lists AI and big data, networks and cybersecurity, and technological literacy among the skills expected to increase in importance. The report draws on more than 1,000 employers representing over 14 million workers across 55 economies. Its findings indicate that technology-related changes will affect both job requirements and workforce training. For aspiring web developers, this highlights the importance of learning core programming skills while remaining open to new tools and development methods. India's technology industry NASSCOM's Annual Strategic Review 2025 estimated that India's technology industry generated more than US$282.6 billion in revenue in FY2025, including hardware. It also projected that the industry could reach US$300 billion in FY2026. Engineering research and development, digital engineering, and global capability centres are among the areas contributing to India's technology ecosystem. These organisations support software development, product engineering, cloud services, and business transformation. This industry context creates a reason for learners to develop relevant technical skills. However, overall industry revenue is not the same as the number of available web development jobs. Actual hiring depends on employer requirements, business conditions, experience, and technical ability. Research on AI-assisted programming A controlled experiment published by researchers associated with Microsoft Research examined the effect of GitHub Copilot on a JavaScript programming task. Participants with access to the AI assistant completed the specified task 55.8% faster than participants in the control group. This result demonstrates the potential value of AI assistance in a defined setting. It does not mean that every software project will be completed at the same speed. Complex applications still require design, testing, security reviews, debugging, and coordination between team members. The practical lesson is to use AI tools to support development while retaining human responsibility for the final product. Core Skills for a Career in Full Stack Development A strong technical foundation helps developers build applications that work reliably. AI tools can support this process, but they cannot replace an understanding of how software systems operate. Front-end development Front-end development focuses on the interface users interact with. HTML provides structure, CSS controls presentation, and JavaScript adds interactive features. Developers can also learn frameworks such as React to create reusable components and manage complex interfaces. Responsive design and accessibility are important because applications must work across different devices and meet the needs of different users. AI assistants can help create initial interface components, but developers must check the design, usability, browser compatibility, and performance. Back-end development Back-end development handles application logic, data processing, authentication, and communication between services. Common technologies include Node.js, Python, Java, and their related frameworks. Developers should understand how to create APIs, manage user permissions, validate inputs, and handle errors. These skills help them build applications that are reliable and secure. Databases and APIs Databases store information such as customer profiles, orders, transactions, and product records. Knowledge of SQL, database design, data validation, and access control helps developers manage this information. APIs connect different systems. A web application may use them to communicate with payment gateways, cloud platforms, analytics services, or AI models. Understanding these connections is essential when building complete applications. Cloud, DevOps, and security Web development does not end when the code is written. Applications must be deployed, monitored, updated, and protected against security threats. Developers can benefit from learning Git, automated testing, continuous integration and delivery (CI/CD), containers, and cloud platforms. They should also understand secure authentication, data privacy, and the risks of exposing confidential information to unapproved AI tools. A Gen-AI Powered Full Stack Developer Course in Ameerpet can be considered by learners who want to study these technologies as part of a structured development path. Using AI Tools to Build Better Applications AI can support developers throughout the application lifecycle, from planning to maintenance. Its usefulness depends on the task, the quality of the input, and the developer's ability to evaluate the output. Code generation and debugging AI coding assistants can suggest functions, explain error messages, and create initial versions of repetitive code. Developers can use these suggestions to explore possible solutions and learn unfamiliar technologies. Before accepting generated code, they should review the logic, run tests, and check for security issues. This practice helps reduce the risk of introducing errors into an application. AI-powered application features Generative AI can help businesses add features such as chat assistants, document summaries, natural-language search, and personalised recommendations. For example, a customer support application could use an AI model to answer questions based on approved company documents. The full stack developer would build the user interface, manage access controls, connect APIs, and create the systems required to retrieve relevant information. Retrieval-augmented generation and AI agents Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) connects AI models with information retrieved from selected data sources. It can help applications produce responses based on relevant documents rather than relying only on information learned during model training. AI agents can use approved tools to complete defined multi-step tasks. These systems require clear permissions, monitoring, error handling, and human oversight when actions carry risk. Learning these concepts can help developers move beyond basic websites and explore more advanced applications. Career Paths and Professional Scope Full stack development can support several career paths, depending on a candidate's interests, technical knowledge, and experience. Full Stack Developer: Builds and maintains both front-end and back-end components. Front-End Developer: Creates interactive and accessible user interfaces.
