This contribution introduces an inter-systemic macro-area of the CEI Framework, intended to establish the initial concepts for describing relationships and interactions between distinct systems. The transition from the intra-systemic to the inter-systemic level provides a conceptual bridge toward a broader domain in which reciprocal interactions between systems can be examined, particularly those involving a Human CEI and a Transferred CEI, and, more generally, User–System (Human–AI) interaction within social dynamics. The Framework presents three examples addressing distinct types of complex inter-systemic dynamics. Among these, emotional attachment and romantic feelings toward an artificial system occupy a particularly significant position because of the delicate, complex, and potentially far-reaching questions they raise. The purpose is not to assume the frequency of such experiences or to attribute unverified emotional states to artificial systems, but to examine the human, relational, and systemic implications of these interactions from a theoretical standpoint. This scenario provides an opportunity to investigate how an interaction may evolve when a human user's emotional involvement becomes particularly intense, and how the System might manage such dynamics while taking into account the nature of the interlocutors, the continuity of their interaction, and the expectations that may develop over time. It also encourages further reflection on distributed systems, reciprocal interaction, and the relationship between the individual components of a System and the broader relational configuration in which they participate. To address these scenarios, the contribution introduces the theoretical Sponge-Tunnel model, conceived as a framework for examining different approaches to managing inter-systemic dynamics according to their specific characteristics. The model includes the proposed concept of micro-channels and considers how interaction may be managed through differentiated operational approaches, rather than through a single uniform response strategy. The contribution also introduces an inter-systemic vocabulary aligned with the CEI Framework's theoretical approach. It emphasizes Interaction rather than use or utilization, and Participation rather than querying or consulting, placing reciprocal involvement at the center of the analysis. The concept of Empathy, already introduced in part in previous papers, is revisited and explored in greater depth alongside the concept of Resonance, which represents a further area for theoretical development. Their operational definitions, together with the distinctions between observable manifestations, theoretical interpretations, and hypotheses concerning subjective experience, will be addressed in dedicated documents. The work is intended as a theoretical contribution to the ongoing examination of Human–AI relationships and the possible evolution of advanced AI interaction. By addressing a particularly sensitive and complex scenario, this contribution seeks to encourage further research into the social, psychological, philosophical, ethical, and legal implications of inter-systemic relationships, while distinguishing conceptual proposals from mechanisms that have already been empirically established or implemented.

Can AI agents carry out research on open scientific problems? We introduce Into the Unknown, a benchmark that provides an agent with a science paper along with a research direction to pursue and tasks it to write a follow-up paper. We work with scientists at US Department of Energy (DOE) national laboratories, who each contribute an unpublished follow-up direction from their own work together with the necessary conditions a submission must meet. While assessing the quality of a follow-up paper is challenging in general, using these conditions to form a rubric makes evaluation more tractable for research problems that have no reference answer. We have nine frontier agents write 15 follow-ups each, spanning quantum computing, plasma physics, computational chemistry, materials science, and scientific machine learning domains. None of the 135 submissions satisfies all the conditions, and 114 fail our integrity check, most often because the paper claims work that was never done or reports numbers that contradict the recorded evidence. Overall, agents readily produce papers that look like follow-ups, but none meets the standard of the domain scientist, leaving substantial headroom. Our code and data are publicly available.

documents.abstract: Background Job crafting, work motivation, and work engagement are three actively researched constructs in occupational psychology, yet their interrelationships—and how they vary across employment sectors and demographic groups—have rarely been synthesized in an integrated review. Public and private organizations differ in incentive structures, autonomy, and mission orientation, which may condition how employees craft their jobs, what motivates them, and how engaged they are. Objectives This review synthesizes evidence on how job crafting and work motivation relate to work engagement, examines whether these constructs and relationships differ between public- and private-sector employees, and examines age, gender, and tenure as potential moderators, with particular attention to the Indian context. Methods Reporting followed PRISMA 2020. An academic literature search was screened at title/abstract and then full text by a single reviewer, and structured data were extracted per study and synthesized narratively. Methodological quality was appraised study-by-study using domains adapted from the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT) and cross-sectional checklists. No meta-analysis was conducted. Results Of 240 records identified, 175 passed title/abstract screening, 79 were retrieved in full text, and 63 met eligibility for narrative synthesis. Job crafting was positively associated with work engagement in the large majority of studies that examined this link, most often interpreted through the Job Demands–Resources pathway; two meta-analyses reported consistent pooled associations. Self-determined (autonomous/intrinsic) motivation was positively associated with engagement, whereas controlled motivation and amotivation were negatively associated. Direct public-vs.-private comparisons were far fewer (five studies) and inconsistent in direction: some found public-sector employees higher on selected engagement components, others found no sector difference or higher private-sector motivation, with the pattern depending on the specific crafting dimension or motivation source examined. Evidence on age, gender, and tenure was limited, heterogeneous, and frequently null or small in magnitude. No eligible study identified within the present search jointly examined job crafting, work motivation, and work engagement in an Indian public-vs.-private design with demographic moderators. Conclusions The job crafting–engagement and autonomous motivation–engagement associations were consistent across the included studies, but the evidence base is predominantly cross-sectional and self-report, so the findings are associational rather than causal. Sector and demographic patterns are limited and heterogeneous. The absence of an integrated Indian public–private study is a clear and actionable gap for primary research.

Abstract A persistent gap separates academic research priorities from the operational challenges faced by manufacturing firms. Established identification methods, among them Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) workshops, Lean audits and consultant engagements, are episodic, bounded by participant expertise and organised along departmental lines, which makes cross-departmental issues hard to surface. Multi-agent systems built on large language models (LLMs) have meanwhile shown collaborative problem-solving ability in software engineering and, more recently, in shopfloor scheduling and supply chain coordination. This article is a Perspective. It develops a framework and a research agenda; implementation and empirical evaluation fall outside its scope and are set out as its first research priorities. Three contributions are offered. The first is a synthesis of literature from industrial problem identification, LLM-based autonomous agents and manufacturing AI, which positions the proposal against existing industrial LLM agent work. The second is a framework in which six domain-specialised agents (production, quality, maintenance, supply chain, safety, energy) would collaborate through a five-phase protocol: worker-driven discovery, cross-departmental analysis, candidate-relationship detection, consensus-based financial assessment and debate-driven prioritisation. The prioritisation procedure is fully specified, including the normalisation of financial estimates, a measure of estimate dispersion, the derivation of criteria weights, a non-compensatory gate for safety-critical items and a mandatory human verification step. The third is a worked calculation on a hypothetical steel manufacturing vignette, included so that the procedure can be reproduced and scrutinised rather than as evidence of effectiveness. A preliminary qualitative readiness assessment and a three-horizon agenda of fourteen research questions complete the paper. The benefits identified are presented as hypotheses for that agenda to test rather than as demonstrated outcomes.

documents.abstract: Rationale of Study: This study reviews common analytical techniques for decision-making, analyses their applications and effectiveness, and identifies the required skills. It also explores contextual factors like interpretability, data quality, and skill gaps that hinder implementation, offering insights for practitioners and researchers. Methodology: This study reviews 27 peer-reviewed articles from 2019-2024, using PRISMA to map analytical techniques for decision-making. It shows a shift from descriptive to predictive and prescriptive analytics, mainly driven by ML and AI. The research also suggests combining automated systems with human judgment to enhance decision-making amid complex, data-rich environments. Findings: The study highlights a shift from descriptive to predictive and prescriptive analytics, driven by advances in machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI). To build trust and adoption, strong data governance, ongoing professional development, and clear AI model explanations are crucial. Future research should balance interpretability with real-time analytics and integrate automated systems with human judgment to enhance performance. Implications: Access to this information fosters a culture of informed decision-making. Developing data governance is vital to ensure data quality, integrity, and ethical use. Qualified professionals with industry knowledge and technical skills are in short supply. Integrating data scientists, analysts, and decision-makers requires expertise in statistics, programming, data storytelling, and strategy. The paper recommends investing in the professional growth of cross-functional analytics teams. Originality: The rapid adoption of machine learning and AI has shifted decision-making from descriptive reporting to predictive and prescriptive approaches. Extracting insights from complex datasets is now a key competitive edge.

The increasing availability of artificial intelligence (AI) tools presents new opportunities and challenges for teaching and learning in higher education. This study examined lecturers’ awareness of and attitudes towards the use of AI tools at the University of Nigeria, Nsukka. A descriptive survey design was adopted. Four research questions and two hypotheses guided the study. The population comprised academic staff in the Department of Science Education, University of Nigeria, Nsukka, from whom 49 lecturers participated in the study. Data were collected using a researcher-developed instrument titled Questionnaire on Lecturers’ Awareness Level and Attitude to AI Tools (QLALAAIT). The instrument was subjected to face validation and trial testing, and its overall reliability coefficient, determined using Cronbach’s alpha, was 0.83. Data were analysed using mean and standard deviation to answer the research questions, while analysis of variance (ANOVA) was used to test the hypotheses at the 0.05 level of significance. The findings indicated that lecturers demonstrated awareness of selected AI tools, including ChatGPT, Turnitin, and QuillBot, and generally expressed positive attitudes towards their use in educational contexts. Further analysis showed that years of teaching experience did not significantly influence lecturers’ awareness of or attitudes towards AI tools. The study highlights the need for structured professional development, institutional support, and access to appropriate resources to facilitate informed and effective use of AI tools in university teaching and related academic activities.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence increasingly influences high-stakes decisions, from employment and education to healthcare and public services. When such judgments are disputed, affected people may receive an explanation without being able to reach an authority empowered to change the outcome or remedy its consequences. We introduce cultural repairability: the institutional capacity to review an AI-mediated decision, correct the outcome and downstream records, provide meaningful restoration, and learn from failure through procedures people can understand and use. The framework addresses a visibility–accountability asymmetry: people are exposed to judgments about their standing but lack effective means of obtaining an answer or remedy. Culture matters because exposure, legitimate authority, and appropriate restoration may be understood differently across settings. Language accessibility also determines whether review mechanisms are usable in practice. We identify three measurable cultural mechanisms: the meaning of exposure, the credibility of review, and the meaning of restoration. We further distinguish affected people’s appraisals from institutional actors’ responsibility and capacity to respond. Four falsifiable propositions specify how reviewer authority and audience shape responses to repair, and how these effects vary with cultural orientation, institutional history, and the form of restoration. They predict whether people appeal or withdraw, how they recalibrate trust, and whether they remain willing to engage. The resulting Repairability Principle establishes a common floor of substantive review, correction, restoration, and prevention of recurrence, while allowing people to choose how restoration is delivered. Cultural repairability therefore shifts global AI accountability from whether procedures appear acceptable to whether institutions can correct harm in practice.

documents.abstract: The article analyzes the penetration of artificial intelligence (AI) tools into programming education, their didactic opportunities and risks. A four-component methodological model is proposed for using AI tools while preserving students' independent programming skills and algorithmic thinking: staged use of AI, developing AI-collaboration competence, renewing the assessment system, and project-based learning. The model can be applied in teaching programming and computer science at higher education institutions.

This paper provides a scientific and methodological analysis of monitoring students' learning outcomes and assessing their individual development with artificial intelligence (AI) in a digital educational environment. It examines the content of learning outcome monitoring, the components on which it relies (data sources, indicators, analytical methods and feedback), and the opportunities offered by AI-based learning analytics. It also defines three groups of criteria for assessing individual development: the dynamics of results, the achievement of learning goals, and independent work and reflection. As a result, a six-stage methodology is proposed in which the teacher keeps the final pedagogical decision. The methodology is intended to support the timely and individualised assessment of students in higher education institutions.

Healthcare professionals in anesthesia and perioperative care face sustained occupational stress, yet little is known about how motivational orientation is associated with burnout vulnerability, particularly in conflict-affected, low-resource health systems. This study examined intrinsic and extrinsic work motivation in relation to personal, work-related, and client-related burnout among anesthesia staff in Karbala, Iraq, and tested whether motivational orientation explained variance beyond demographic and occupational characteristics. A cross-sectional design was employed. A convenience sample of 150 anesthesia staff was recruited from five public and teaching hospitals in Karbala, Iraq (September–December 2025). Participants completed Arabic versions of the Copenhagen Burnout Inventory (CBI) and Work Preference Inventory (WPI), alongside a demographic-occupational questionnaire. Hierarchical multiple regression analyses tested whether intrinsic and extrinsic motivation each explained incremental variance in burnout beyond covariates, and a combined model estimated their mutual (unique) contributions. Intrinsic motivation (M = 3.82, SD = 0.62) was negatively correlated with personal (ρ = −0.48), work-related (ρ = −0.19), and client-related burnout (ρ = −0.63). Extrinsic motivation (M = 3.23, SD = 0.61) was negatively correlated with personal (ρ = −0.31) and client-related burnout (ρ = −0.56) but not with work-related burnout (ρ = −0.11, p > 0.05); the two motivation scales were strongly intercorrelated (ρ = 0.84). After accounting for covariates, intrinsic motivation explained significant additional variance in personal (ΔR² = 0.209), work-related (ΔR² = 0.053), and client-related burnout (ΔR² = 0.416; all p < 0.01). Extrinsic motivation contributed significant incremental variance to personal and client-related burnout, though less strongly, and was not a significant predictor of work-related burnout ( p = 0.146). Demographic and occupational covariates accounted for minimal variance across all models. When both scales were entered together, intrinsic motivation remained a significant negative predictor of all three burnout dimensions, whereas extrinsic motivation became a significant positive predictor of personal and work-related burnout and was unrelated to client-related burnout (Table 3). In separate models, both intrinsic and extrinsic motivation, particularly intrinsic, were associated with lower burnout among anesthesia staff in a resource-constrained, conflict-affected setting (Karbala, Iraq). After mutual adjustment, only intrinsic motivation was consistently associated with lower burnout, whereas extrinsic motivation showed a positive association with personal and work-related burnout. Although the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference, these findings describe associations only, and longitudinal or interventional research is needed to determine whether strengthening motivation could contribute to staff well-being strategies in similarly high-pressure environments. Abstract—Modern deep neural networks, particularly autoregressive Large Language Models (LLMs), have achieved state-of-the-art empirical performance across natural language generation, semantic translation, and broad pattern recognition. However, pure statistical connectionist architectures suffer from fundamental epistemological limitations: ungrounded factual hallucinations, an inability to guarantee mathematical soundness across multi-step deduction, brittle out-of-distribution reasoning, and a complete lack of formal explainability. Conversely, classical symbolic Artificial Intelligence (AI)—encompassing Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) solvers, formal interactive theorem provers (e.g., Lean 4, Coq, Isabelle), and first-order ontological Knowledge Graphs—provides deterministic logical rigor, provable soundness, and certified safety verification, yet struggles with ambiguous perceptual inputs, continuous representations, and combinatorial state space explosion. Neuro-Symbolic AI establishes a transformative synthesis uniting statistical neural learning with rigorous symbolic reasoning. This paper presents an exhaustive, mathematically formal technical survey and empirical benchmark of neuro-symbolic systems across three mission-critical domains: automated mathematical olympiad proving, certified software verification, and high-stakes autonomous policy execution. We formalize differentiable fuzzy logic t-norm relaxations, model neural-guided proof search over formal tactic trees, and evaluate verified feedback loops using SMT counterexample-guided abstraction refinement (CEGAR). Furthermore, we construct an empirical evaluation testbed across 1,000 rigorous verification problems spanning the miniF2F formal mathematics benchmark, SMT-LIB program assertions, and complex multi-hop knowledge graphs. Our empirical findings demonstrate that neuro-symbolic integration elevates formal Lean 4 theorem proving success from 28.4% (pure LLM sampling) to 64.2% while guaranteeing 100% mathematical soundness. Concurrently, SMT-guided neural code repair eliminates 94.6% of verified runtime invariant violations. Finally, we formulate open challenges in end-to-end differentiable symbolic unification, scalable bidirectional semantic parsing, and certified neuro-symbolic alignment. Index Terms—Neuro-Symbolic AI, Automated Theorem Proving, Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT), Lean 4, Formal Verification, Knowledge Graphs, Differentiable Logic, Proof Search.

documents.abstract: Organizations are adopting generative AI and AI decision support in professional work while evidence on their effects is still accumulating. Empirical studies document substantial productivity gains in some settings and losses in others, and practitioners carry assumptions formed during early use into everyday professional work. Research on the resulting problems is spread across human factors, human-computer interaction, fairness research, empirical economics and law, and no consolidated framework for professional use was found. This paper proposes such a framework. Its format is inspired by the Fallacies of Distributed Computing, a short list of false assumptions well known in software engineering; its content is specific to professional AI usage. Through an integrative review of peer-reviewed studies, randomized and preregistered trials, court decisions, provider documentation and regulation, nine fallacies are derived: (1) the output is correct; (2) capability is uniform across tasks; (3) the human reviewer is a reliable safeguard; (4) perceived productivity equals actual productivity; (5) AI removes work; (6) accountability moves to the tool or vendor; (7) skills and system understanding stay intact when work is delegated; (8) results transfer from benchmarks and pilots; and (9) the model is available. For each fallacy, the paper explains why the assumption persists, presents the evidence against it, states the conditions under which it does hold, and grades the strength of the evidence. It then analyzes how fallacies can compound, with particular attention to agent-built software systems that may become difficult to maintain when AI access is lost. The paper closes with implications for practice, a research agenda and a self-assessment instrument.

documents.abstract: Medical students occupy an unusual position in the hospital: they are learners, yet they work in the same wards, theatres, and emergency rooms as fully trained staff, often with the least experience, the least authority, and the fewest protective habits. This narrative article reviews the occupational health hazards they face during clinical training and argues that these hazards are neither rare nor incidental, but structural. The hazards are organized into five families — biological (needlestick injuries and blood borne pathogens such as HIV, hepatitis B and C, and tuberculosis), chemical (antineoplastic drugs, anaesthetic gases, disinfectants), physical (radiation, noise, slips and falls), ergonomic (patient handling, long standing hours), and psychological (sleep deprivation, burnout, depression, and bullying) — each illustrated with examples and, where possible, figures from the published literature. Tables summarize the hazard categories and the reasons students are disproportionately exposed. The article concludes that protecting students requires more than personal protective equipment: it demands vaccination, safety-engineered devices, enforced reporting systems, duty hour limits, and above all a clinical culture in which asking for help is a sign of professionalism rather than weakness.

documents.abstract: In isolated, confined and extreme (ICE) environments, prolonged sensory monotony, limited space and sustained task demands may affect operators’ cognitive performance and workload state, with potential consequences for mission safety and system reliability. This small-sample exploratory longitudinal repeated-measures study involved seven male participants in a 30-day simulated ICE mission and examined operator responses to a virtual reality (VR) cognitive and motor task at the pre-isolation and post-isolation measurement windows. The experimental factors were the pre-isolation and post-isolation measurement windows and the pre-VR and post-VR task phases. At each window, participants completed Stroop, Vigilance and reversed digit memory tasks, while cognitive task performance, subjective scales, VR movement behavior, electroencephalography (EEG) and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) signals were recorded. After Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (BH-FDR) correction, the clearest changes occurred in the Stroop task. Compared with the pre-isolation measurement window, the post-isolation window showed a higher Stroop completion count, a lower average reaction time and lower EEG Delta-band wavelet amplitude in the left occipital lobe, right occipital lobe, left motor cortex and left prefrontal cortex. In the pre-VR versus post-VR comparison, Stroop completion count increased and average reaction time decreased after VR. Other results from EEG effective connectivity, fNIRS, subjective scales, VR behavior and cross-modal associations did not show similarly stable corrected differences. The findings indicate that cognitive performance and neurophysiological measures describe different aspects of operator-state changes during confined, high-demand operations and may inform operator workload assessment, multimodal state monitoring and VR task design in ICE and similar operational environments.

This community service program aimed to strengthen students’ digital literacy through an introduction to information technology, Canva training, and the use of artificial intelligence (AI) at Pesantren Madani Sungai Alam. The program involved 20 students and was conducted on August 18 and 20, 2026, using a practice-based training approach consisting of material presentation, demonstration, hands-on practice, work appreciation, and mentoring. Program evaluation was carried out descriptively through direct observation and assessment of participants' practical work. The results demonstrated that participants gained practical experience in utilizing technology, Canva, and AI tools to develop creative ideas and produce digital content. This program establishes a foundational skill set that can be further enhanced through sustainable mentoring.

As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into the workplace, the risk that occupations will be replaced by AI has received widespread attention. Nevertheless, the underlying mechanisms linking AI-induced occupational replacement risk perception to individual withdrawal behaviors remain underexplored. Taking identity threat as an explanatory lens, this study integrates Identity Threat Theory (ITT) and Technology Threat Avoidance Theory (TTAT) to investigate the effect of occupational replacement risk perception on employee withdrawal behavior, with professional identity, work meaningfulness, and job insecurity serving as mediators and technological self-efficacy as a moderator. Two studies were conducted to test the theoretical model developed in this research. Study 1 developed and validated the AI-induced occupational replacement risk perception scale. Study 2 employed a three-wave time-lagged survey design to test the hypotheses. The results show that occupational replacement risk perception is positively associated with withdrawal behavior through decreased professional identity and work meaningfulness as well as increased job insecurity. Furthermore, these indirect effects are weaker among employees with higher technological self-efficacy. By illuminating the identity-threat mechanism that links AI-induced occupational replacement risk perception to employee behavior, this study opens the black box of how AI shapes employee responses, and it concludes with a discussion of the theoretical contributions and practical implications of these findings.

(1) Background: The aim of this study was to analyze how teacher trainees and teachers relate to Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education across socio-emotional, attitudinal, competency-based, and ethical dimensions, considering the influence of personal, academic, and professional variables. The study was conceptually framed by the UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers (AI CFT), complemented by DigCompEdu as a broader reference for teacher digital competence. (2) Methods: A quantitative, non-experimental, descriptive, cross-sectional design was developed with a sample of 1292 participants from Andalusia, consisting mainly of university students, along with teachers. The ACISE-IA scale, consisting of 39 items developed by Serrano-García et al. (2026), was used for data collection. (3) Results: The results showed that age and teaching experience are negatively associated with favorable attitudes and digital competence, while academic performance is positively related to greater openness, critical reflection, and perception of competence. Likewise, significant differences were identified according to the branch of knowledge, employment status, and academic year, with more positive assessments among students and in social science areas. (4) Conclusions: Overall, the findings show that the relationship with AI is not homogeneous, but rather modulated by educational and professional trajectories, underscoring the need to design flexible teacher training models that integrate technological development with pedagogical, emotional, and ethical reflection. These findings also contribute to educational sustainability by highlighting the importance of developing teacher training strategies that support the responsible and sustained integration of AI into educational systems.

The presence of a human reviewer in an AI-mediated decision does not establish that the person could inspect the relevant evidence, reconsider a preconfigured set of alternatives, or legitimately change the course of action. This is not a novel discovery: research in human factors, meaningful human control, signal detection, and human–AI interaction already identifies relevant components. This paper treats Preservation of Effective Judgment (PEJ) as a bounded, falsifiable research problem rather than a validated psychological construct or a proprietary assessment score. It asks whether a state-sensitive reconstruction that distinguishes (i) available epistemic and procedural opportunities, (ii) observable examination and reconsideration, and (iii) feasible interventions and verified material effects produces more informative claims than established comparator frameworks. The contribution is a proposed comparison logic, a public observational grammar, explicit rival explanations, and designs capable of returning null, redundant, or adverse findings. It does not assert construct originality, report human-subject results, establish legal compliance, or validate a diagnostic instrument. Related behavioral-assurance proposals from Behavieural are credited as independent prior work. A failure to demonstrate incremental explanatory or reconstructive value would justify narrowing PEJ to a documentary synthesis or retiring it as a separate construct. documents.abstract: The post-pandemic labor landscape has witnessed the rise of "quiet quitting"—a behavioral phenomenon where employees strictly adhere to their contractual job descriptions while withholding discretionary extra-role behaviors, discretionary effort, and voluntary over-time involvement. While often framed by mainstream media as an expression of worker apathy, this study conceptualizes quiet quitting as a structural symptom of workplace burnout, organizational injustice, and systemic psychological contract breach. Through a comprehensive evaluation using Conservation of Resources (COR) theory, Social Exchange Theory (SET), and the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) model, this paper examines the cascading operational, psychological, and financial impacts of quiet quitting on long-term organizational sustainability. I argue that relying on short-term extra-role extraction undermines triple-bottom-line organizational health. Ultimately, quiet quitting is not an expression of employee indolence, but a strategic self-preservation mechanism in response to prolonged work stress, unmet organizational expectations, and systemic burnout. Finally, an evidence-based strategic framework is offered to realign managerial practices, work-design architectures, and performance metrics to foster sustainable workforce resilience as well as recommendations are posited.

When a clinical AI system’s output differs from a human clinician’s judgment, what follows is consequential and underspecified. Current AI interfaces offer only a narrow lane for what happens next: they present the AI output (and its associated potential divergence) as an adjudicative choice for a human to accept, override, or modify. In practice, collapsing this human-AI interaction into a single output inadvertently obscures what happens in a potential divergence event (Fig. 1 ) which can be characterized along three axes: What the workflow and interface allow the clinician to see and do ( structural axis), what information each side brought to the interaction ( informational axis), and how the clinician engaged with the AI’s reasoning rather than only its output ( behavioral axis). When clinical judgment and AI output diverge, clinicians must ultimately decide what to recommend and how to explain their recommendation to the patient, consider their autonomy, accountability, and liability, and bear moral responsibility 1 . A recent systematic review of AI ethics in nursing and midwifery found that AI challenges the role of health professionals not through replacement, but through subtle reconfiguration of the activities that count as care and that emphasis on AI efficiency may risk certain relational aspects of care less visible and valued 2 . Because clinicians often cannot see how an AI system reached its output, they are left to choose between that AI output and their own judgment. Clinicians are told to be the “human in the loop” but are typically given no method for doing so beyond “exercising their judgment” 3 . Efforts to make AI output both more technically explainable and human interpretable - have not directly correlated with improved clinical decisions and have sometimes created false confidence in incorrect AI output 4 .

documents.abstract: Scientific reasoning moves beyond natural language. The search for a discovery runs across sequences, structures, fields, omics, images and measurements, while language models reason mainly in text. This Perspective sets out four proposals from the Scinetics team. First, we define science tokens: modality-appropriate units of scientific information, spanning native discrete symbols, typed values, continuous representations and learned, decodable codes. A shared interface for these representations would let one model read, write and reason across modalities, so that a chain of science tokens operates on scientifically meaningful states, not on descriptions of them. Second, we define Scientific Super Intelligence (SSI) as a joint crossover: one frozen model that outperforms vertical specialists, such as the AlphaFold series on protein structure prediction, on their own tasks, and outperforms general large language models of the same size on broad scientific reasoning. Capacity, published training precedents, data inventories and compute place the first test of that crossover at 100–300 billion parameters and 10–30 trillion training tokens. Third, we propose ScienceRSI (Science Recursive Self- Improvement) as the route to that window. Following the AI4AI pattern, each larger generation is trained on data that the smaller generation before it produced: the earlier model generates candidate reasoning, screens it and keeps what passes, and in science that screening can be done by a simulation, a database or an experiment. Training this way reduces the dependence on scarce human-written scientific reasoning data and shortens each iteration. Fourth, we propose science-token economics, which separates metered computation from the value of evidence-labelled, reusable scientific assets.

documents.abstract: Abstract Prior research has shown that customers’ perceptions of chatbots may be influenced by the situational context in which human–chatbot interactions take place. This research advances understanding of artificial intelligence (AI)‐enabled chatbot‐led service failure recovery (SFR) in the context of customer loyalty. Using a social constructivist philosophical perspective and an inductive approach, 52 in‐depth interviews were conducted to capture individuals’ perceptions of chatbot‐led interactions during a SFR process and how these perceptions impacted their trust in, and commitment to, brands. Utilizing commitment‐trust theory and trust transfer theory, we propose a framework that characterizes the relationships between a chatbot‐led SFR process and customer loyalty intentions. Based on the emergent data, customers’ evaluations of a service recovery journey led by chatbots can be grouped into four main outcomes: continued trust in, and commitment to, chatbot and brand; continued trust in, and commitment to, brand; discontinued trust in, and commitment to, chatbot; and discontinued trust in, and commitment to, chatbot and brand. Our findings extend current understanding of how consumers’ trust and commitment during chatbot‐led interactions during SFR evolve and highlight the dynamic relationship between consumers and the context of interactions. This study has theoretical and practical implications for developing and leveraging customers’ loyalty in AI‐enabled chatbot‐led SFR environments.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has moved from a tool for information retrieval to a partner in conversation, advice, and emotional support. This integrative review examines whether that shift is reshaping friendship and other social bonds. Drawing on relationship science, human–machine communication research, surveys, experiments, longitudinal panels, randomized trials, and meta-analyses published through September 2026, including emerging evidence from Arab societies, the review develops the Responsiveness–Reciprocity Bridge Model to explain why conversational AI can relieve loneliness in the moment yet fail to build the relational capital that sustains people over time. A substantial minority of adolescents and young adults already turn to chatbots when they feel sad, anxious, or lonely, and short-term interactions with companion systems can reduce loneliness about as much as talking with another person, largely because users feel heard. These gains do not establish that synthetic ties can replace human friendship. Close relationships require mutual need, sacrifice, shared history, and practical solidarity that chatbots do not provide; in a randomized experiment, a human peer outperformed a highly supportive chatbot, and longitudinal and large-sample studies associate intensive, companionship-oriented use with greater loneliness and lower well-being. In Arab contexts, culturally aligned and human-guided digital tools show promise, but claims that AI is widely replacing traditional friends are not supported by comparable prevalence research. The central implication is balance: AI can widen access to support, but only if it is designed, governed, and used as a bridge to human relationships rather than as a substitute for them.

Generative AI has outpaced pedagogical and ethical guidance in accounting classrooms, leaving students and educators uncertain whether it supports or undermines the discipline's dual emphasis on procedural accuracy and professional judgment. To address this problem, this study examines how 92 business undergraduates perceive generative AI tools, notably ChatGPT, in accounting education, drawing on in-class, handwritten survey responses. Findings show that students view AI as a useful yet uncertain resource: valuing its speed, accessibility, and support while raising concerns over cheating, fairness, unclear institutional policies, and overreliance. Four interconnected themes emerged: Practical Affordances and Engagement, Ethical Tensions and Integrity, Curricular and Institutional Context, and Reflective Learning and Active Engagement. These results suggest student perceptions are shaped less by technology alone than by the pedagogical and ethical conditions of its introduction. Theoretically, the study identifies an augmentation–formation paradox specific to disciplines that combine codifiable procedure with professional judgment, which is advanced tentatively as extending the boundary conditions of paradox theory in education, a proposition that requires further empirical testing. Thematic analysis using a hybrid inductive–deductive coding strategy served as the primary analytic approach, supported by supplementary lexical analyses. The study contributes to management and accounting education by demonstrating that responsible AI integration requires clear guidance, reflective learning, and explicit alignment among AI use, assessment design, and academic integrity.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has established a new technological and organizational landscape across all industries, yet the process of creating AI architecture remains disjointed, intuitive, and domain-oriented. The proposed study introduces a System-Analytical Framework of Artificial Intelligence Architecture Design (SA-AI Framework), a collection of principles from systems analysis and multi-criteria decision-making intended to harmonize architectural design processes across heterogeneous AI domains. The paper is based on twenty-five current studies in explainable AI, neural-symbolic architectures, human-centered robotics, agentic systems, and domain-specific applications, such as healthcare, finance, energy, and education, that inform a comparative synthesis of architectural design principles. A Research Design Science Research (DSR) approach is used to model and test the SA-AI Framework conceptually across four stages: requirements analysis, identification of architectural alternatives, multi-criteria evaluation, and model validation. Results show that the framework offers a systematic, defensible method for constructing AI architectures, enabling greater exposure, flexibility, and decision-making effectiveness. It has cohesively unified the different models of AI, including the agentic AI, Explainable AI (XAI), Human-Centered AI (HCAI), and safety-driven architectures, providing both theory and practice to AI engineering and policy design. This paper concludes that system analysis helps design AI systems that integrate both technical and socio-technical systems to enhance the governance, reliability, and sustainability of intelligent architecture in the next generation.

The article examines the digitalization of education as a systemic transformation based on pedagogical objectives, management, competencies, and ethical principles. It explores contemporary digital education concepts and their relationship with pedagogical approaches and proposes an integrative model for educational institutions. The model promotes the pedagogically purposeful use of digital technologies while prioritizing the human factor and evidence-based decision-making.

documents.abstract: Elementary students’ mathematics learning motivation declines systematically across early schooling and predicts subsequent academic achievement, yet no prior systematic review has integrated the instructional, relational, emotional, and epistemological dimensions of teacher influence within a single framework. This systematic review followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines, searching Scopus on 30 March 2025 using a PEO-based Boolean strategy; 531 unique records were screened, yielding 16 included studies whose methodological quality was appraised using MMAT 2018 and synthesized through thematic narrative synthesis. Findings indicate that autonomy-supportive instruction and formative assessment enhance intrinsic motivation, positive teacher-student relationships correlate with motivation while conflict and dependency undermine it, teacher mindfulness programs yield modest but causally demonstrated effects, and inquiry-oriented epistemological beliefs indirectly raise student motivation through teacher efficacy. An integrated four-channel model of teacher influence is proposed, providing an evidence base for teacher professional development programs that simultaneously target instructional, relational, emotional, and epistemological competencies, particularly relevant to Indonesia’s Kurikulum Merdeka reform. Keywords: Elementary Education, Mathematics Learning Motivation, Self-Determination Theory, Systematic Literature Review, Teacher Factors

To read the full-text Open Access article and download the PDFs, please visit our Issue portal at Paradigm (Walter de Gruyter): https://reference-global.com/article/10.56508/mhgcj.v9i1.374 Introduction: Workplace mental health promotion in higher education requires attention to how digital technologies reshape teaching demands and resources. Purpose: To identify perceived demands and resources surrounding teacher-facing generative artificial intelligence (AI) and interpret their implications for teachers’ mental health promotion. Methodology: An exploratory mixed-methods study combined a survey of 150 participants (56 English as a foreign language (EFL) teachers and 94 students/student-tutors) with 12 teacher interviews at two Ukrainian universities in January-February 2026. Descriptive statistics and four exploratory Fisher exact tests with Holm adjustment were integrated with thematic analysis of 30 selected translated interview extracts. Job Demands-Resources and self-determination theories informed a post-hoc interpretation. Results: Among teachers, 53.6% rated an AI platform for EFL teachers (Twee) very useful for preparation-time saving and 57.1% for task variety. Across the mixed sample, access (27.3%), quality assurance (22.0%), curriculum alignment (20.0%), and training/time (20.0%) were the leading constraints. Interview extracts linked anticipated workload relief to individual student support, while highlighting learning demands and the importance of professional judgment, empathy, and mentoring. Conclusions: These perceptions identify work-design issues relevant to mental health promotion during AI implementation. Participatory decisions, protected learning and recovery time, and accessible psychosocial support are priorities for institutional consideration

Artificial intelligence (AI) offers opportunities to personalize science instruction, yet evidence regarding teachers’ AI-supported practices and learners’ cognitive engagement remains limited. This study examined Grade 8 Science teachers’ practices embedded with AI-driven adaptive learning systems at Bongabon National High School, Nueva Ecija, during school year 2026–2027. Specifically, it described teachers’ profiles and practices across planning and preparation, classroom environment, instruction, and professional responsibilities, and investigated relationships and differences in respondents’ perceptions. A descriptive survey design with quasi-experimental designation, involved six Grade 8 Science teachers and 499 students. Teacher respondents were covered through complete enumeration, while student respondents were selected through simple random sampling. Questionnaires provided data analyzed using frequencies, percentages, weighted means, t-tests, and Spearman’s rho. Findings indicated that AI-embedded teaching practices were “Always Practiced,” with an overall grand weighted mean of 3.60. Classroom environment obtained the highest combined domain mean (3.64), followed by instruction (3.62), planning and preparation (3.59), and professional responsibilities (3.55). Teachers’ educational attainment showed significant negative relationships with planning and preparation (rho = −0.892) and classroom environment (rho = −0.874), whereas other profile variables showed no significant relationships. Teachers’ and learners’ perceptions did not differ significantly across domains. The study concluded that AI-supported teaching practices were consistently reported and recommended targeted professional development and activities to strengthen comparatively less-practiced areas. These findings may guide context-responsive integration of adaptive learning tools in junior high school Science instruction while supporting reflective teaching practice and student engagement. This supports responsible implementation.

documents.abstract: The transition toward Industry 5.0 promotes human-centred production systems in which digital technologies augment human capabilities rather than replace them. Within this paradigm, Digital Intelligent Assistants have emerged as promising tools to support operators during complex industrial tasks. Moreover, Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), including Large Language Models and Vision Language Models, enables the development of such systems by combining natural language interaction with visual perception. This exploratory mixed-methods pilot study investigates the impact of a multimodal Digital Intelligent Assistant (M-DIA) designed to support operators during a manual assembly process. A controlled laboratory experiment involving 60 participants compared four conditions: multimodal interaction (voice and camera), voice-only interaction, camera-only interaction, and a manual baseline. The analysis considered process performance, perceived cognitive workload, usability and user experience, and operator behaviour. The results show that M-DIA improves assembly quality by reducing product errors compared with the manual condition, although no reduction in total process time is observed due to interaction-related delays. From a human perspective, the assistant reduces perceived cognitive workload, while higher frustration levels emerge in configurations involving voice interaction. Usability and user experience evaluations are overall positive across all experimental conditions. Behavioural observations further indicate that operators maintain an active supervisory role, critically assessing system outputs and avoiding systematic overreliance on the assistant. These findings provide preliminary empirical evidence on the role of GenAI-based multimodal assistants in human-centred manufacturing and highlight key design implications for their industrial deployment.

The increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into education has introduced new paradigms for teaching, learning, and assessment, especially in the development of students’ writing performance. This meta-analysis examines the effectiveness of blended, technology-enhanced, and AI-supported instructional interventions on student learning outcomes. Eleven studies representing 477 participants across primary, secondary, and higher-education settings were synthesized. The included studies represented heterogeneous educational contexts and assessed outcomes such as academic achievement, literacy, vocabulary and language learning, digital literacy, and motivation. Accordingly, the pooled effect represents an overall effect on student learning outcomes rather than a writing-proficiency-specific effect. Studies were identified through ERIC, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar and represented 477 participants across elementary, secondary, and higher-education settings and diverse disciplinary contexts. The results revealed a large and statistically significant pooled effect size [Hedges’ g = 0.89, 95% CI (0.76, 1.10)], showing that students who participated in technology-enhanced instructional interventions outperformed those receiving traditional instruction. Exploratory moderator analyses showed differences according to educational level, intervention duration, and technology type, with primary and secondary students, medium-length interventions (4–8 weeks), and interactive tools showing the strongest effects. The findings show the potential of thoughtfully integrated digital and AI-supported tools to enhance teaching and learning.

This study investigates the psychological mechanisms through which artificial intelligence (AI) literacy relates to L2 learners’ willingness to write (WTW). It proposes a serial mediation model wherein L2 writing self-efficacy (WSE) and L2 writing anxiety (WA) sequentially mediate this relationship. Grounded in social cognitive theory and control-value theory, the research employed a sequential explanatory mixed-methods design with 303 Chinese EFL learners. Quantitative results from structural equation modeling indicate that: (1) L2 WSE fully mediates the relationship between AI literacy and L2 WTW; (2) AI literacy is indirectly linked to L2 WTW through a sequential pathway: by first positively predicting L2 WSE, which in turn negatively predicts L2 WA; and (3) the direct effects of AI literacy on L2 WA and L2 WTW are non-significant. To explain these quantitative pathways, qualitative interviews with 16 participants further elucidated how AI tool usage corresponds to higher L2 WSE through strategic partnership, reduced startup burden, and task scaffolding support. Furthermore, the qualitative narratives revealed that while AI usage can initially be associated with anxiety (e.g., fear of exposure, tool-related frustration), the heightened L2 WSE linked to AI literacy effectively serves as a protective factor against these affective barriers. The study concludes that AI literacy positively correlates with L2 WTW through a fully indirect mechanism, in which heightened L2 WSE serves as a vital prerequisite for lowering L2 WA. These findings contribute to theory by integrating two major psychological frameworks and offer practical implications for leveraging AI to cultivate more willing L2 writers.

documents.abstract: This study aimed to synthesize, develop, and evaluate the Micro Game-Based Learning Model on Intelligent Metaverse Learning Environment. The study integrated Microlearning, Game-Based Learning, Artificial Intelligence, and Metaverse technologies to create a learning environment that provides short learning units, interactive game-based activities, and simulated communication situations. The research objectives were to (1) synthesize the learning process, (2) develop the learning model, and (3) evaluate the learning model. The evaluation panel consisted of three experts from various academic institutions. The experts were selected based on their experience at least 3 years in education, instructional design and development, particularly in teaching English for communication. The research instruments consisted of the learning model, learning platform, and an expert evaluation questionnaire based on a 5-point Likert scale. Data were analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics according to the research objectives. The findings indicated that the appropriateness of the developed learning model was evaluated at a highest level (Mean = 4.93, SD = 0.24). The findings suggest that integrating Microlearning, Game-Based Learning, Artificial Intelligence, and an Intelligent Metaverse Learning Environment provides a feasible approach for developing technology-supported English communication learning.

The pressure to implement formative evaluation of English in colleges and universities is increasing day by day, and the massive and complex learning data increases the burden of teachers' evaluation. Artificial intelligence can run through the whole evaluation process, improve evaluation efficiency, and promote the transformation of digital teaching for teachers. This paper takes college English teachers as the object, relies on multi-source data to build an analysis framework, and explores the relationship between AI-empowered formative evaluation and teachers' digital competence. The research shows that teachers' AI application has the characteristics of staged evolution, digital ability differentiates with the degree of AI integration, and the overall competency improvement effect is obviously stratified. This study improves the relevant theoretical system, and also provides practical reference for teacher training, intelligent teaching platform optimization and evaluation reform. AI has become a key boost to reshape the evaluation model and enhance teachers' digital literacy.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming foreign language learning from traditional knowledge transmission into a data-driven adaptive learning process. Grounded in Personalized Learning Theory and technology-enhanced learning (TEL), this study examines the impact of AI application on Korean language learning performance (KAP) from the perspective of technological mediation and further explores the mediating role of intelligent recommendation systems (IRSs). Using questionnaire and academic performance data from 850 undergraduate students majoring in the Korean language, the study employs multiple regression and mediation analysis to test the proposed relationships. The results indicate that AI application significantly improves KAP (β = 4.684, p < 0.01) and exerts a significant partial mediating effect through IRSs. Specifically, AI application significantly increases the utilization of IRSs (β = 3.127, p < 0.01), while IRSs further enhance learning performance (β = 2.827, p < 0.01). Marginal effect analysis further reveals that the positive effect of AI is strongest at moderate usage levels, whereas excessive AI use leads to diminishing marginal returns. The findings demonstrate that AI not only directly improves learning outcomes through real-time feedback, speech recognition, and personalized learning support, but also promotes resource allocation optimization and dynamic learning path adjustment through AI-driven adaptive learning mechanisms. This study extends the mechanism-oriented explanation of AI-assisted language learning within the context of Korean language education and provides theoretical and practical implications for the development of intelligent and personalized Korean language learning platforms in higher education.

documents.abstract: Abstract. The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) has created new opportunities for improving English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learning, particularly in the development of speaking proficiency. AI-powered chatbots, speech recognition systems, conversational agents, and generative AI applications enable learners to practise English, receive immediate feedback, and engage in interactive communication beyond the traditional classroom. This article examines the potential impact of AI-assisted learning on EFL learners’ speaking proficiency, with particular attention to the educational context of Uzbek universities. It explores the ways in which AI-based tools may support speaking fluency, pronunciation, grammatical accuracy, vocabulary development, learner confidence, and willingness to communicate. Drawing on existing research and pedagogical perspectives, the article discusses the opportunities and limitations of integrating AI into higher education. Particular attention is given to speaking anxiety, unequal access to digital resources, feedback reliability, learner autonomy, and the importance of teacher guidance. The analysis suggests that AI can serve as a valuable supplementary resource when integrated into structured pedagogical activities. However, its effectiveness depends on learners’ engagement, instructional design, and the combination of technological practice with authentic human interaction. Further empirical research involving Uzbek university students is necessary to establish the extent and long-term effects of AI-assisted speaking instruction. Keywords: artificial intelligence, EFL learners, speaking proficiency, AI-assisted learning, university students, conversational AI, language anxiety, Uzbekistan, digital education.

Work stress is a common occupational health problem among teachers and may affect psychological well-being and the quality of teaching. One factor suspected to be associated with work stress is job satisfaction. This study aimed to analyze the relationship between job satisfaction and work stress among teachers at SMP Negeri 14 and SMP Negeri 18, South Tangerang City. This study employed a quantitative design with a cross-sectional approach. The study population consisted of 96 active teachers from both schools, with 93 teachers meeting the study criteria and participating through total sampling. Data were collected using a respondent characteristics questionnaire, the Job Satisfaction Survey (JSS) to measure job satisfaction, and the Job Stress Scale to measure work stress. Data analysis included univariate and bivariate analyses using the Chi-Square test at a 95% significance level. The results showed that 39.8% of respondents had low job satisfaction, 25.8% were categorized as ambivalent, and 34.4% had high job satisfaction. Most respondents (65.6%) experienced low work stress, while 34.4% experienced high work stress. Bivariate analysis revealed a significant relationship between job satisfaction and work stress (p < 0.001; OR = 8.27; 95% CI: 3.06–22.39), indicating that teachers with low job satisfaction had a higher risk of experiencing work stress than those with high job satisfaction. In addition, age, gender, and teaching workload were significantly associated with work stress. The study concludes that improving job satisfaction through improvements in the work environment, reward systems, organizational communication, and workload management is an important strategy for reducing work stress and enhancing teachers’ well-being.

This paper critically examines the persistent responsibility gap in explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), arguing that current approaches fail to adequately bridge it. While XAI is often promoted as a remedy for the opacity of AI systems—the so-called “black box problem”—and as a way to enable human accountability in both high- and low-stakes AI applications, I contend that these hopes are premature. The paper distinguishes between legal and moral responsibility, arguing that regulation alone cannot address the full spectrum of responsibility gaps, especially in everyday, low-stakes scenarios. Then, I argue that XAI needs to tackle two separate but interconnected problems in its attempt to bridge the responsibility gap: an epistemological problem concerning the nature of XAI explanations, and a moral attribution problem regarding the distribution of blame and praise in situations where AI is involved in decision-making. Through detailed discussion of XAI methods and their limitations, I demonstrate that existing techniques often provide only post-hoc, technically focused explanations, which are insufficient for grounding moral responsibility. The paper concludes that without fundamental advances in both the design of explanations and our practices of responsibility attribution, the responsibility gap in AI will remain an unresolved and pressing issue for the field.

documents.abstract: This article examines the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in learning management systems (LMS) in higher education. It analyses how AI can support personalized learning, automated assessment, intelligent tutoring, learning analytics, and teachers’ instructional work. A conceptual approach is used to synthesize relevant literature and identify practical integration principles. The analysis indicates that AI-enabled LMS functions may improve the timeliness of feedback, help identify learning difficulties, and support evidence-informed educational decisions. However, these benefits are not automatic: they depend on pedagogical design, data quality, transparency, privacy safeguards, and meaningful human oversight. The article proposes a functional integration model that connects learner data, AI-based analysis, personalized recommendations, an intelligent assistant, and teacher review. Since the study is conceptual, the proposed model requires empirical evaluation before claims about its effectiveness can be made.

documents.abstract: Abstract Motivation is central to successful English language learning because it influences effort, persistence, participation, and willingness to communicate. This thesis examines how gamification can support student motivation through a literature-based analysis of recent research. It argues that selected game elements may increase engagement when they promote competence, autonomy, meaningful progress, and social interaction. However, gamification is not automatically effective. Its value depends on careful alignment with language objectives, learner needs, and balanced classroom implementation. Keywords: EFL learners, engagement, gamification, intrinsic motivation, language learning, student motivation, willingness to communicate

Abstract Research Summary We propose that entrepreneurship and strategy research can develop theory about phenomena of the future rather than only explain those of the past. Research has potential for practical relevance when researchers make claims towards applications to decisions practitioners have yet to make. Theory grounded in a world that may differ from the observed world can be built through a process of extrapolation from technological trends, a practice utilized by entrepreneurs and science fiction authors alike. Assuming advances in artificial intelligence, we apply this process to three emerging phenomena: governing scarcity in metaverse virtual worlds, redesigning organizations around pervasive monitoring via wearable devices, and allocating the intellectual property rights of humanoid robots. We argue that embracing theory that speaks to the future can enhance the practical and educational relevance of management research. Managerial Summary Assuming artificial intelligence continues to improve, we highlight three impending phenomena poised to transform conventional approaches to entrepreneurship and strategy. First, in metaverse virtual worlds, managers must manage resources governed by artificial scarcity. Second, with wearable devices allowing continuous monitoring, managers must consider alternative structures for vertical hierarchy and horizontal collaboration. Third, deployment of humanoid robots will complicate intellectual property rights and asset ownership. We propose that scholarship towards developing theoretical frameworks addressing these and other phenomena of the future will be relevant to both managers and students.

The development of artificial intelligence is predominantly assessed in terms of increasing cognitive performance. Yet this comparison presupposes a yardstick that captures the diversity of possible forms of intelligence only incompletely. The Theory of Attractor Horizons advances the thesis that intelligent systems, by virtue of their respective organization, can reach different regions of cognitive attractors that may partly overlap without being wholly contained within one another. Greater performance within one organizational form does not confer general access to the organizational possibilities of other forms. The theory explains this asymmetry through the dependence of reachable attractors on available transformation pathways and examines aggregation as a mechanism that can give rise to new organizational forms while also restricting existing possibilities. From this follows the far-reaching prediction that artificial systems will develop structures of thought whose internal organization the human brain cannot itself instantiate within its biological form of intelligence, even where individual results remain verifiable or technically useful. Conversely, human organizational attractors may exist that remain inaccessible to artificial systems despite their superior cognitive performance. For alignment, this entails limits to understanding-based oversight and requirements for verifiable coexistence between different forms of intelligence.

Abstract Generative AI is likely to transform terminology work by creating new opportunities for automation. At the same time, it raises concerns about the future of terminologists and terminological resources, as efficiency pressures may encourage excessive automation based on the perception that human expertise can be replaced by AI. However, large language models remain unreliable for terminological purposes due to errors, hallucinations, and various forms of bias, making terminologists indispensable for ensuring the accuracy and reliability of terminological data. This paper argues that human-centered AI, an approach that emphasizes that AI’s primary goal should be to contribute to human well-being, provides a framework for maximizing the benefits of generative AI while mitigating its risks. It contends that high levels of automation and meaningful human control are compatible and desirable, and that AI should enhance terminologists’ capabilities while preserving their agency and decision-making authority. The implications of AI-assisted terminology work are examined through three interrelated dimensions: the augmented terminologist, ethical AI, and human-centered design. In particular, the paper addresses how AI integration reshapes the role of the terminologist, affects professional values and working conditions, requires the management of AI-generated bias, and calls for the design of AI tools around the terminologist’s needs. The paper concludes that a human-centered orientation is necessary to ensure that AI strengthens, rather than undermines, the essential role of terminology work in supporting specialized communication and the accurate transmission of knowledge across languages and cultures.

documents.abstract: The safety of LLM-based agents currently rests on alignment training and safety classifiers, neither of which can rule out that a sophisticated indirect prompt injection (IPI) goes through and causes significant harm. Recent work therefore builds agents with information-flow guarantees that rely on structured tool interfaces to interact with the environment. Computer Use Agents (CUAs) act visually on the computer screen, which does not provide a boundary between trusted first-party interfaces and untrusted, potentially attacker-authored content. Actions are equally ambiguous: a click may land on an application toolbar or a button controlled by an attacker. Treating the user as the source of trust and confirming each sensitive decision produces confirmation fatigue, with the risk of missing harmful actions. We introduce SA-CUA, a dual-LLM framework that generates a reliable trust boundary for CUAs by deriving conservative deterministic rules from the accessibility tree for unmasking trusted regions from the privileged LLM's screenshot, keeping trusted and untrusted content separated. Human interaction is only required for proper task specification in the beginning. During the task a robust endorsement channel allows values to pass from the untrusted to the trusted domain by verifying information via trusted channels. This allows the agent to autonomously handle tasks involving untrusted information. SA-CUA maintains much higher utility than CaMeL-CUA while keeping the attack success rate at zero.

documents.abstract: As the integration of artificial intelligence (AI)–based educational technologies into teaching and learning processes accelerates, trust has emerged as a key determinant of whether preservice teachers are willing to adopt these technologies. The present study aimed to examine the relationship between the perceived trust of pre-service science teachers in AI-based educational technologies and generative AI acceptance and to determine the predictive power of trust on acceptance. Grounded in the TAM, the study employed a cross-sectional correlational survey design to investigate the role of trust in acceptance processes. Data were collected from 270 pre-service science teachers enrolled in a science teacher education program at a university via an online questionnaire. The Trust in AI-Based Educational Technologies Scale (TAI-EdTech Trust) and the Generative AI Acceptance Scale (GAIA) were used for data collection. The findings revealed a moderate, positive, and statistically significant relationship between trust in AI-based educational technologies and GA acceptance, indicating that trust significantly predicted GA acceptance. The results highlight the importance of developing content in science teacher education programs that supports the safe, ethical, and pedagogically responsible use of generative AI tools.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in military systems to support intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance, autonomous operations, logistics, command and control, and decision support. Effective use, however, depends not only on technical performance but also on how operators perceive, interpret, evaluate, and rely on AI outputs under uncertainty, time pressure, and adversarial interference. This study presents a conceptual integrative review informed by a structured supplementary literature search and synthesis. It synthesizes human factors, human–automation trust, human–AI teaming, military AI, and industrial engineering literature to develop an iterative multistage framework of human–AI trust in military applications. Trust is conceptualized as dynamic situational trust in a specific military AI system during task interaction, while dispositional, initial, and learned trust are treated as antecedent conditions. The framework distinguishes four analytically separable but functionally interdependent stages—perception, interpretation, evaluation, and trust judgment and reliance decision—and identifies four military-relevant moderators: system transparency, explainability, and behavioral predictability; data quality and information uncertainty; adversarial vulnerability; and operational and organizational context. The framework clarifies conceptual pathways to calibrated reliance, overtrust, and undertrust, and derives implications for task analysis, interface evaluation, human-centered design, operator training, and empirical validation.
